utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it is with deep regret that I have formally to announce that Judge Robinson's wife has died recently. I'm sure we would all wish to express our condolences to the Judge. In the circumstances, he will be away for the next fortnight and will not return until the 24th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, all those present will extend our sympathy and condolences to the Judge both through Your Honour and maybe privately. I think I can probably speak for all of us in recording the silent admiration we had for what we must all have appreciated was the suffering he was engaged in but silently and without in any way being distracted from the work that he put in on this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we will ensure that what you've said is conveyed to the Judge. I turn next to the proposed programme for the next two weeks. The new Rule 15 bis provides that if a Judge, for illness or other urgent personal reasons, is unable to continue sitting in a part-heard case for a period which is likely to be of short duration and the remaining Judges of the Chamber are satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so, those remaining Judges may order the hearing of the case continue in the absence of the Judge for a period of not more than three days. We have considered that Rule and are of the view that it's in the interests of justice to continue this hearing this week for three days, but we'll hear any submissions that anybody wants to make about that. Thursday and Friday of this week are in any event set aside for hearings on ex parte matters and we will have to consider in due course whether it's right to continue those hearings, although at the moment we would be minded if possible to do so. Next week this case is listed for four days of hearings and we will consider whether it's possible and hear any submissions as to whether it's possible to continue for those days. Does anybody want to make any submissions about those proposals?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not on that point, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It's a shame that we have to start the new millennium on this somber note, and please, please give our condolences to Judge Robinson in the appropriate way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I will see that that is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Our position, frankly, is as to the next week, that it would be a hardship, it may be a hardship to proceed only because it means even more of an imposition on Judge Robinson to read the record, to see the record. For those reasons we've pondered it, and while everyone, of course, is anxious to proceed, we think it in the best interest perhaps not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as this week is concerned, you have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Absolutely none. Absolutely none. Three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you've taken the view that three days the following week would impose, you say, a hardship upon the Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I don't want to speak and I shouldn't speak for him, but three days plus another three or four days, and there are some other days that he was absent, there comes a point, and Your Honour can best judge, when it's burdensome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we took an opposite view, would you have any other observations to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if in principle we're going to work next week, I have no observations to make. If we're not going to be sitting next week, I have witnesses to cancel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll obviously have to consider that and consider it in the next day or two in light of the submissions made, and we will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I tell you what the position is about witnesses because I know that informally last week there was some concern that there may have been inadequate witnesses to fill the three days that we have for evidence this week. Today there's a witness called Breljas who will take some time but along with all other witnesses will, I hope, be taken as quickly as possible. Then there's two other witnesses called Van der Pluijm and de Boer, neither of whom I hope will be particularly long. There were listed for this week two witnesses for whom subpoenas had been issued, and the Chamber will recall, as it were, a rolling programme of subpoena witnesses, two this week, two next week, and I think one the week after, were the return dates for those witnesses. The two for this week have not responded, and there's a report before the Chamber explaining why they have not responded. So this week would be the time when the Chamber can take further steps to secure their attendance if the Chamber judges it right to do so. I would rather not deal with that matter now and would rather get on with the evidence of Breljas for two reasons: first, so that we can consider the matter a little more following the effective start of the whole team being together again this week; second, to ensure that any institutional opinion of the OTP generally on inviting the Chamber to use its full powers to bring witnesses to court can be reflected in the submissions I make. Of course, I act independently in this trial but I'm obliged from time to time to check that there isn't an institutional view that it would be desired I lay before you. Perhaps we can deal with that either tomorrow or Wednesday. There is the potential for additional witnesses this week, three in particular, I think. First, there is the aerial video of the Lasva Valley taken a couple of years after incidents but when the damage was still more apparent on the ground than it is today, and there's a witness called J.P. Capelle, who although he wasn't actually on the flight, I think commissioned the flight and knows the area extremely well, who would be able to sit here while the video is being played, the videotape is about 40 minutes, and give evidence of identification of particular villages save wherever that's necessary, and it's only necessary to a limited extent because the video actually has the names of the villages appearing in print at the bottom of the screen as the helicopter moves from one village to the next. So that's one passage of evidence that we could deal with but, of course, in a way it's a bit of evidence that one would probably want Judge Robinson to see at the same time as Your Honours were seeing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that must be right and I think that would be more appropriately dealt with when the Judge is back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. There are two other live witnesses whose summaries were prepared last week and served last week who may be available. One is (redacted). I say he may be available. I haven't been able to check on his availability. He was a listed witness. There is another witness called Beese, who was not a listed witness and accordingly for whom there is inevitably objection by the Defence, but who is available and could be here on Wednesday. Christopher Beese was the deputy to a witness who gave evidence in closed session, but it was that witness who first pointed us, both informally and indeed in Court, to the extreme help that this witness Beese might be able to give to the Chamber. The Chamber will know that in relation to that confidential witness, we had no direct access to him and weren't even able to speak to him informally until the moment that he came to Court. So we couldn't get his guidance on where information might be most usefully found. And he told us then about how we should approach Beese. We did that. And indeed he is a very valuable witness, potentially a very valuable witness, not a particularly lengthy one, for two reasons: One, he is the first-hand observer of an encounter by telephone between Kordic and Petkovic, which simply shows where the power lay. And since there's been objection to this material whenever it comes secondhand, it would be hard to see what objection there can be to producing the evidence when it comes first-hand. Second, from his very considerable contacts on the ground, he has conclusions, well founded it may be thought, about the conduct and purpose of the war. The Chamber may note when looking at the summary, because I am going to ask that the Chamber should have the summary presented to it, and we can discuss the possibility of his being called, perhaps later today or tomorrow. The Chamber may find that his opinions don't necessarily match exactly all the other opinions that have been ventured. But that, of course, is not a bad thing. On the contrary, it's a good thing, because what we seek to do for the Prosecution is not to argue some narrowly constructed case and to be selective in the material we lay before you, but to lay before you the best evidence from all those who necessarily had different perspectives on the conflict, having confidence that the Chamber will be able to decide from those opinions and general expressions of factual finding where the truth lies. So Beese would be available. I need to tee him up probably really this afternoon. So that we will serve on you, if it hasn't been done already, the summary of his evidence, which was served on the Defence last week. Perhaps we can discuss the possibility of calling him this afternoon when we see how Breljas is doing and how long he is going to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before Breljas is called, I should say this about the tape recording that was served on the Defence at the end of last year, with an invitation that they might admit that the voices on it were Kordic and Blaskic. No response has been made to that invitation so far. Breljas is a man who would probably be able to identify one or other of the voices, Blaskic and Kordic. For reasons to do with this institution, the evidence unit in which all these important things are stored hasn't been available to us last week. And I haven't been able to get the tape and have it played to Breljas before he starts giving evidence this morning. There may come a time today, I hope, when the tape will be available to me again, and I would ask the opportunity that it be played to him so that we know whether he will be able to help with voice identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there a dispute about the tape or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The tape creates problems, Your Honour, and the problems are these: First, it's an incomplete tape. There obviously had been some sort of interception, some sort of wire-tap interception. And this is only part of it. It's our position we are entitled to see all of the tape or tapes of wire-tapped intercepts, first issue. The second issue is it creates a legal issue of the admissibility of evidence which, if I am correct, was subject to a wire-tap, legally or illegally, with or without a warrant. And if I read the tea leaves correctly, it's without a warrant. Under Bosnian law at the time, it would be illegal and should not be played anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That aside, of course, that will be a matter of argument as to admissibility. The narrow issue is whether there is any dispute about the voices on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: There is a dispute about the voices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In those circumstances, if I may have an opportunity at some stage, assuming the tape becomes available to me again today, to have it played to Mr. Breljas, to see if he is able to help with the identification, I would be grateful. We might indeed put that in at the same time as we are dealing with the arguments about calling Mr. Beese, the additional witness, sometime this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear the arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the dispute is that the tape is not complete. The tape we believe to be chopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I take that. But the issue here is whoever the voices on the tape are. That's the matter which is in dispute, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Actually, no. If you listen to the tape and then compare the tape with Mr. Kordic's voice on other tapes that you've seen, I think you can make your own judgement. I don't think this witness is needed to do that. Our issue is the accuracy of the tape itself. While I am on my feet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Stein, may I follow this, because it's important as far as today's hearing is concerned. Are you saying that it's accepted that the voice is Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So there is no need for the Prosecution to call evidence on that narrow issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whether, of course, it's admissible and what's in it, those are totally different issues which we will have to resolve.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As to, in reverse order, Mr. Beese, again not a listed witness, not only not listed but given to us kind of by surprise in our packet of material over the recess. We were told there would be three witnesses this week, and we certainly are not prepared to deal with him this afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When did you get his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It was in my possession when I came back to The Hague on Thursday, so presumably before. I mean, I'll accept whatever date Ms. Verhaag tells us she sent it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as you are concerned, you didn't receive it until Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Last, while I'm on my feet, the Prosecutor apparently has made a report on subpoenas. I don't know if it's appropriate for us to see that report, but we haven't, for whatever his institutional reasons are. That's not been given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I'm not sure you are entitled to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I agree. As to Mr. Beese, there was no statement from him because we weren't on his trail until pointed to him by the witness I've identified. He was seen by me in London last week and, as soon as a summary was prepared, I think it was Thursday, it was faxed to The Hague and then delivered to the boxes of the Defence counsel the same day. But, in any event, when the Chamber has a look at the summary, it will be in a position to decide the degree to which the factual matters referred to are new and would take them by surprise this week. Three other points. On the tape, I understand what Mr. Stein says to be an acknowledgment that the voice of Kordic is Kordic where said on the transcript, and Blaskic where Blaskic is identified on the transcript. That being the case, then I needn't, of course, have the tape played to Mr. Breljas, because it's unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On Thursday, as the Chamber knows, there is a binding order application. There's been quite a lot of correspondence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The short point, a short point on Mr. Beese, so that you can take account of it, is this: As Judge Bennouna points out, more time may be needed before the Defence are in a position to deal with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it may be that the notion of calling him this week is not appropriate in any event. Perhaps you would like to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly understand that. Dealing with it step by step. If the Chamber has a look at the summary, and if the Defence raised discrete arguments about matters that are new in this witness that haven't been touched on by other witnesses, then indeed they may have an unarguable case for him not to be dealt with this week. But I was responding in making him available as a potential witness to the concerns that have been informally expressed by the Chamber. Two other points then. Binding order material on Thursday, application on Thursday. There's been a considerable amount of correspondence since last year about that hearing and about, frankly, who should be here. I don't think I'll go into that now, because we want to get on with the evidence. But the issues are there still to be dealt with and they are not issues that are going to go away. I can, however, console the Chamber with this: The binding order application material is very voluminous. I hold my hand up. I think it's about that thick at the moment in the way it comes, although some of it is duplicative. I am having prepared a chronology which so far is only about four sides in tabulated form, which I hope will guide you through the history of the binding order; complex, as it is, covering two cases as it does. And I think that that will, if not save you having to read all of the material, guide you through it in a way that will be -- will make it economic, your disposal of time on that issue. That will help. We are waiting for a skeleton argument on the inadmissibility of the witness Cigar that has yet to arrive. There was concern by the Chamber, I think possibly informally expressed, about core documents. Can I inform the Court that we are substantially through the exercise of identifying all the remaining exhibits we would want in, including the core exhibits, as, if you will, the library of documents to which parties might refer in closing argument; they not necessarily being documents each and every one of which would have to be turned through laboriously, but they would need to be available. A large number of those, a large proportion of those indeed has already been served on the Defence for them to agree in principle that they are documents to be admitted. The rest, I think, will be turned over to the Defence by the end of this month. I am looking to Mr. Lopez-Terres because I think he has been engaged in this. I think by the end of this month, before the end of this month. It is hoped, one way or another, that the vast majority of documents that we seek to lay before the Chamber, for the purposes of the library to be available, will be dealt with by consent, and that only a limited number of documents will have to be the subject of full argument as to provenance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There must be a distinction between the library of documents, which I take to mean all the exhibits which are already voluminous and in numerous files. That is inconvenient from the point of view of reference in Court to have this large number. So I would encourage anybody to produce a core bundle which we can use during argument and that sort of thing. It will, of course, contain documents from both sides. It's not intended that it should merely be one side. At the end of the Prosecution it may be necessary to carry out a full exercise to make sure that all the exhibits are exhibited, that we have the right numbers for them, and that we can proceed in an orderly fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I think that the logging of exhibits already produced has been comprehensive and accurate. And if we add to that, by those documents served and to be served on the Defence, then there is no reason to think that we shouldn't be in a position to document the library accurately. The notion of a core bundle for use in argument is not one I had formally understood. I thought that reference to core documents had been to the core documents served with the opening. It seems Your Honour's idea is, if I may say so, a very good one and one to which we will be responsive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: One nagging point relative to Mr. Van der Pluijm. Apparently there are annexes to his statements and we would like to have those before he appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we call the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that the Defence has given us a list of the paragraphs with regard to which they wish us to ask questions in a traditional manner rather than in a leading manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You are, indeed, Mr. Anto Breljas, born on the 19th of January, 1940 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: On the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, you are a Croat from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, were you sentenced for any criminal offences in the past?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, never seriously, but once in 1971 when I joined the Croatian string in Zagreb, I had to flee to Canada. When I reached Canada, I was provoked by a priest who was plundering the Croatian people in the name of Croathood, but he was really a thug. I had a fight with him. Then in court he lied that I wanted to physically assault him, but the court then sentenced me to three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were you sentenced to prison, to a prison term at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I was, for three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: For physical assault.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Breljas, you belonged to the special purpose unit known as the Vitezovi, the Knights, I think, in your language.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, from 1993, from the 3rd or 4th of March until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Until April 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. About the 15th of April I left the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, at the end of March, 1993, you met the accused Dario Kordic in Tisovac, outside Busovaca, and you asked him whether he could give you an assignment within the HVO forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Not an assignment. I just reported to him; I told him I had arrived and that I wanted to join.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And Mr. Kordic told you to go and see the head of the Vitezovi, Darko Kraljevic, explaining to you that this one would give you a job within the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber in what capacity you joined the Vitezovi. What were your functions?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: At first, for four or five days, there wasn't anything really, I just observed things, and afterwards I was a political officer in the information and propaganda unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: An information and propaganda officer within the unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What rank were you given when you joined the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: The rank of lieutenant. Not immediately, but about ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe your duties as an information and propaganda officer, in a few words, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: According to the rules of international organisations and international conventions, the IPD officer had to make sure and monitor things that were done properly and incorrectly. If possible, he should prevent any errors and praise anything that was done well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were also in charge of the social problems of the soldiers in the unit, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. I was also -- Jozo Buha was the logistics man. He stole a lot and I prevented that and threw him out. Kraljevic followed my advice, and then I had to take over the logistics for the Vitezovi as I had no other person to assign to that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were you also in charge of taking care of the families of killed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I was able, I would distribute food to them. When I received packages, I would distribute those packages to the wounded and the families of the killed, and on two occasions, I also received some funds which I distributed to both groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were also responsible for the treatment of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I was responsible for the prisoners; I had to take care of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the course of your duties, you also acted as a liaison officer with international organisations, and as you spoke English, you were known as UNPROFORac, that is, the liaison man with the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. On a number of occasions, I was asked to interpret because there weren't many people speaking both English and our language.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Breljas, what was, in your opinion, the total strength of the Vitezovi throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: The number changed. There were many casualties and wounded people who were put out of action, and then reinforcements were brought in, and these were assigned by my commander, Marinko Plavcic, so that the number changed. At a maximum, there was 180 and at a minimum, 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And these 180 soldiers were stationed at the Dubravica school, the barracks that were situated in the Dubravica school.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Not all of them. Some were from Krizancevo Selo, and they stayed at home but they came to the barracks. And others who came from other places, like refugees from Travnik and others, they were regularly quartered in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You told us that the commander of the unit was Darko Kraljevic. Who was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: The deputy was Dragan Vinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us how many groups there were forming this unit and the names of those groups?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? I didn't quite understand the question. What do you mean "groups and the names of those groups"? Are you thinking of the fighters, combat groups?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Yes, combat groups that had names.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: There were three main groups: the Pumas, the Wolves, and the Foxes. These names sometimes changed, but basically there were three combat groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You noted in the course of your work that soldiers of the unit wore two types of uniforms; one was a black uniform and another a camouflage uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Not all of them. Some wore black uniforms, they were uniforms they had to make themselves, and the camouflage uniforms were those that were distributed. So that not only my unit but others, like Mr. Blaskic, Mr. Mario Cerkez, they also wore black uniforms, and the Vitez Brigade members also, some of them wore black uniforms, and there were also the camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Is this correct, that the people that were considered to be the most extremist in the Vitezovi had attached on their black uniforms the letter "U" which was the sign of the Ustashas from the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. They either had the letter "U" on the cap or on the side, some of them even or their belts, with the letter "U" on the buckle of their belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There were also official patches with the words "Vitezovi" and another patch with the letters "HOS" on them, with a flash.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Those who were in the HOS, and they were founded in 1990, they all had these HOS patches. However, those of them who joined later, the end of 1992, in December 1992, they didn't wear those patches. They had the "PP Vitezovi" with the flash symbol on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I should like to show you two documents, pictures of those patches, and will you please confirm whether they correspond to the patches worn by some members of the unit or all members of the unit. They are Exhibit Z1530 and Z2790; these are two photographs. Mr. Breljas, was this the official patch of the special purpose unit, the Vitezovi, that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No. The lightning sign is missing, the flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was there another patch with the "HOS" on it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, but the coat of arms had a white background with red squares and not vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The background was reversed?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you show the witness, please, the second document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Does this symbol correspond to the letter "U" for Ustasha that we referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Breljas, we're now going to speak about the night between the 15th and 16th of April, 1993. Could you tell us what you saw in the course of that night while you were at the Dubravica barracks.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening, I had been in Zenica, I had just returned from Zenica, and I learned on the road that Zivko Totic had been arrested. I came in the afternoon, and late in the evening, they came by car to the barracks, there was Mr. Kordic, Darko Kraljevic, and Vinac. There was another person with them but I couldn't describe him precisely for you because I only saw him on one other occasion after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: How many people did you see exactly that evening?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Five or six. Five or six. I couldn't tell you exactly, but five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Apart from the accused Kordic, did all the people in the group belong to the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Except for this one person that I didn't know. He was in the Vitezovi, a second time he came to interrogate some prisoners, but I didn't have him registered in any of my lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, does the name Miso Mijic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Miso Mijic, yes, I always thought that he was the assistant of Darko Kraljevic for SIS, but later on I discovered that Darko Kraljevic was his assistant for SIS. He was a colonel, and that means that he had the same rank as Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was Miso Mijic present that night?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, he was there as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the course of the meeting with the people you have just referred to, Kordic, Kraljevic, Dragan Vinac, Miso Mijic, and another person whose name you can't recall, you were able to see these people talking among themselves, conferring over something.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us what they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what they were talking about exactly. All I can say is that Mr. Kordic said, "That must be done to the end." Then someone answered to that, "Don't worry. Everything will be fine." Who said that is not something I could tell you under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were there any documents that you were able to see where these people were conferring?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No. There was a piece of paper with something drawn on it, some kind of a map on it. Whether they had drawn that map on the spot or whether they had brought it with them, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I should like to show you a document now, Mr. Breljas. You have just referred to Miso Mijic as a participant in the meeting of the night of the 15th and 16th. I will show you a document Z1075.1, "A" for the English version. Mr. Breljas, this document dated the 18th of June 1993, issued by the Security and Information Centre for the Central Bosnia operative zone is signed by Miso Mijic, who appears to be the chief of that centre. Is that the same person who you have referred to, and from this document is it evident that Mr. Darko Kraljevic was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. But I must repeat, I always thought that the situation was the other way around, that he was Kraljevic's deputy and not the other way around. But now I see that I was wrong, that the situation was vice versa. I don't know how I came to that conclusion because Mr. Kraljevic was the commander of the Vitezovi, and whenever I had a list, the list was headed by Colonel Darko Kraljevic, after which came Miso Mijic. And that is why I always thought that Miso Mijic was his deputy. But I now see that that is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, would you clarify, please, what the Central Bosnia SIS Centre is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for your observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, could you tell us once again very briefly what, in your opinion, was the SIS?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I cannot tell you definitely. All I know is that it was the secret police of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Miso Mijic was, in addition to Colonel Blaskic, the head of this SIS service of the Croatia army of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that decidedly. I didn't see any contacts between him and Blaskic, but I do know that he was attached to the Vitezovi. I know that he was there all the time, that he always accompanied Kraljevic. But it is difficult for me to confirm that he had any particular contact with Blaskic. I see from this document that he was, but it is not something that I can confirm. I know that he was a permanent member of the Vitezovi, that he was always with Kraljevic, that he shared the command with Kraljevic, but I couldn't say anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. Within the framework of your duties as an officer for propaganda and information, you participated in the weekly press conferences held by Dario Kordic. Could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Every week, once I had a press conference together with the Blaskic IPD chief, who was the chief of all of us, and also we would go to Busovaca once a week with Dario Kordic and Blaskic, and some other individuals, some would come on and off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did Ignac Kostroman usually participate in those press conferences?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, on a number of occasions. But there was some occasions when he was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Where were these press conferences held, Mr. Breljas?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I don't come from those parts. I come from Sarajevo. But I know that it was in the Busovaca municipality on the first floor in the small hall there. In a hall of the Busovaca town hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of those press conferences you were able to note that the speeches made by the accused Kordic were more or less always the same. Could you tell us what you recollect of the words used by the accused?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. On most occasions he would say, "We have been here for 1.000 years. The tombs of our ancestors are here and we will defend this to the end and succeed in defending it."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you remember what Mr. Kordic wore at those press conferences?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He was very relaxed. He would not allow anyone to provoke him. In my personal opinion, I believe that he wanted to encourage hatred between the Croats and the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But you didn't quite answer my question. But to follow up on what you have said. Did Mr. Kordic regularly refer to the struggle against the Muslims in his speeches at those press conferences?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the leitmotif. He kept talking about the struggle against the Muslims; that we Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina have to fight for survival in our own land, which has been Croatian for a thousand years, and that we must protect the Croatian tombs. That is the gist of what he said and what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The Muslims were described as the aggressors; were they not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I am now going back to my earlier question. That question was what kind of clothes did Mr. Kordic wear? Were they civilian clothes or perhaps military?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, he wore a uniform. He had a large cross on a chain and it was, as a rule, a camouflage uniform. When the weather was warm, then he would have a camouflage shirt. When it grew colder, then it would be a camouflage jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You told us that he had usually two persons with him during those press conferences, that is Mr. Blaskic and Mr. Kostroman at times, but who chaired those press conferences?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: From what I could see and what I knew, it was Mr. Kordic who chaired them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And did you sometimes meet at those press conferences Mr. Anto Valenta too?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. He attended three times or maybe two. I couldn't tell you exactly. But he was there two times that I know for certain, because once I provoked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did Mr. Anto Valenta hold different press conferences at a different place?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. He started to do that somewhat later, perhaps in June or July. In his hotel in Vitez, where the meeting point in Vitez was, in his office. When he was there, that is where he also held press conferences, that is, his own press conferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, we are now sometime in May 1993 and you went to Tisovac again accompanied by a person named Zvonko or Zvonimir Cilic, who was prevalent in the Vitez Brigade, and you were accompanied also by a cameraman of the Vitezovi brigade. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Quite true. I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the purpose of this visit was to attend an interview with the accused, with Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. The IPD of the Vitez Brigade was to make an interview with Mr. Kordic, and the three of us went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I should now like to show you a document, Mr. Breljas, which perhaps has to do something with what I have just told you, and especially the cameraman which you mentioned. It is document Z1153/1. As you can see, Mr. Breljas, this document has a list of names of individuals who were placed at the disposal of the Vitez Brigade and who all belonged to the Radio Television, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And I know most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Precisely. In this list which we will see in this document, could you identify the cameraman of the Vitez Brigade with whom you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stipovic, Srecko Stipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You already spoke about somebody called Marija. Aren't you confused, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, quite true. But later on -- mind you, they all have the same first names, so very often the same surnames. And since I am an outsider, that is how I got confused. So I am quite sure that he is Stipovic. I wasn't sure about the first name, Marijan. Marjanovic was the boss and somehow I connected Stipo (sic) with Marijanovic. And that is what I said, Marijan Stipovic, but that is not true, that is Srecko Stipovic, and I know the man very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. In July 1993, or in summer 1993, you once again met the accused Dario Kordic in Busovaca after a press conference during a pistol handing ceremony --

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Not after the conference, but during, in the course of the conference, during the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I see. And was Colonel Blaskic present too, as well as a military prosecutor, and you told us that his first name was Marinko?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Whether he was already a military prosecutor present there, or did he come later on or was he there before, I'm not quite sure. But Mr. Kordic, that is Colonel Kordic and Blaskic, and the third man -- and a third man. There was somebody else, but I can't really say for that -- it was that. That is Mr. Marinko, he was a prosecutor, but whether he was that at that time, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the purpose of that ceremony was to hand out the pistols, which had just arrived from Croatia, and which had engraved the signature of Mr. Boban, the President?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You had designated two members of the Vitez Brigade who should receive those pistols as a kind of reward?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. The regular units were receiving those pistols for the best soldiers, and because it was up to me to decide who were the best soldiers, I picked out two and took them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the Vitez Brigade was also awarded a prize during that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, but they were more numerous because simply they numbered more men than we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And a little later, in 1993 and towards the end of 1993, Mr. Breljas, you had the opportunity of meeting the accused Dario Kordic in Vitez. Could you tell us something about the circumstances under which you saw Dario Kordic then?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, depends when it was, because I saw him twice. The first time when I had been in Vitezovi, everybody was leaving slowly and I heard that Zabrdze would be attacked. And since my soldiers were up there, who were very good soldiers, because they did not steal ammunition, they were short of ammunition. So at midnight I called the rally point in Vitez where Mr. Sliskovic was on duty, and I told him that I needed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am going to interrupt you, Mr. Breljas, because I am not following this evidence. When was it that this occurred?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: It was sometime in July. And the second time in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to meet Mr. Kordic on the premises of the Impregnacija factory?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. It was in December, in the latter half of December, when the BiH Army attacked Krizancevo Selo. Since Mr. Blaskic was in Mostar, then it was Mr. Kordic who in person lead the defence of Krizancevo Selo and Buhine Kuce. And I arrived with my ten men to defend, that is to try to set up the front. Then I met him at Impregnacija with the commanders of the Vitez Brigade, and they were discussing matters concerning the -- this attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What was Mr. Kordic discussing with the Vitez Brigade commanders at that point?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that, because I was some five or six metres away from them. And I was having trouble with my own men. So that I can't tell you. But he was one of the commanders; that is, there was the area commander and he as his superior. But what they were talking about, I could not hear. And I wasn't really interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could it be that they were discussing the counter-attack after the Muslim offensive?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, that would be the most likely explanation, because they were looking at a map, discussing, so presumably they were talking about how to attack, how to defend. Or what do I know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who was it who was looking at the map, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Kordic and the area commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that the word "Kordic" was omitted from the French interpretation. It was said "Kordic and the area commander," not "Kordic as the area commander," but "Kordic and area commander." Yes, "Kordic and area commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I should now like to show you a document, Mr. Breljas, which is a document drawn up in January 1994 by Major Dragan Vinac, about whom you already spoke to us about. It is Z1380. Will you please look at the last page of that document, the one which bears Mr. Vinac's signature, and where in the last part he speaks about the 22nd of December 1993. Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I can't read it all that fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: That is the penultimate passage above the signature. It says on the 22nd of December 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I can't see it. Oh, yes. Oh, yes. Yes, yes, yes. 22nd December 1993. Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What is the link between this document? Does this document bear on that period of time that you have mentioned when you saw Mr. Kordic at Impregnacija which you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I don't think it was on that particular day. I believe it was likely later, a day or two later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But, in any event, it is a period when you had to provide reinforcements for the Vitez Brigade in order to defend against the attack of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think this was the date of the attack. Two days later, the Vitezovi were reformed so as to come to the rescue of the Vitez Brigade and do a part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And that particular day when you met Mr. Kordic, a representative of the Vitez Brigade, on the premises of Impregnacija in December 1993, was that the first time that you could see, that you realised that Mr. Kordic might also be implicated in activities of a military nature?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, it was not the first time. I was guessing that even before, but I am a rather good strategist and I know the customs of war, and I noticed that he did not really have any strategic military experience but that he also had a say, that he exercised an influence over the troops in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: According to you, was Mr. Kordic on one or another occasion issuing any orders to Darko Kraljevic, your commander?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He could not issue orders to Darko Kraljevic because Darko Kraljevic was a powerful man, but he could indicate to Darko Kraljevic, he could suggest to Darko Kraljevic what should be done and Darko Kraljevic would immediately agree with that end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So your impression was that Darko Kraljevic did not discuss those things which Kordic told him.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, he did not discuss them. All he cared about was the rifle and to launch an attack. He didn't care about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: According to you, when the Vitezovi were sent to the Busovaca area to fight against the Muslims, it was at the request of Dario Kordic, was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. That was in July for the first time. Yes, when they went -- no, not to fight, but to prevent the Muslims from Kacuni where five of our men had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: According to the document which I just showed you, which is signed by Mr. Vinac, there is another passage which I should like you to look at. It is still the Prosecution Exhibit Z1380. The passage I'm concerned about is on page 7 of the English version. This document speaks about -- no, it is page 6 of the English version -- the Vitezovi Brigade which was sent to Prosje, Kacuni, and Busovaca on the 5th of July, 1993, and it is an operation when the Vitezovi suffered fatalities, that is, Miskovic, Vidovic, Kristo, and Kukic were killed.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They were killed then, but it was when Kacuni had already answered with an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And this passage from the report of Mr. Vinac, is it referring to what you told us about, how the Vitezovi men were sent to the area of Kacuni at Kordic's request?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. We're still in the summer of 1993. You met the accused Dario Kordic at the Vitez Hotel, didn't you? You had to see him, you had to discuss a problem with him. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I was not to meet him. I simply came across him by chance, and then I seized the opportunity to ask him something that I had been wanting to ask him for a long time, that is, to send me somewhere else, to remove me, to send me to trenches if need be because I could not stand it any more. The Vitezovi, they were sent there in order to destroy the place and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Dario Kordic answer you that day?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He told me, "Oh, let me be. I've got my problems." When I told him that I wanted to be reassigned to another place, he said, "Just leave me alone. I've got my trouble about."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But did you tell him what was the source, what was the root of the problem?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that later there was the attack from Kacuni because they responded to the provocation. There was an attack against Busovaca, and at that time, Mr. Blaskic was already the commander of the military district, and he was asking Blaskic because only Blaskic could really set the troops in motion, the heavy artillery in motion. Kordic said that he should do so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: -- and Blaskic was the one who started the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, Mr. Kordic asked for the reinforcements and Blaskic responded, "You provoked the Kacuni attack, so you manage it the way you know how."

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is how I put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But let us go back a little bit, Mr. Breljas, to the 16th of April, 1993. That day, you spent the major part of the day with Marinko Plavcic at his command post.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And he said his responsibility covered Krizancevo Selo, Dubravica, and Rijeka; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, not Rijeka really. The Muslims' direction came from Rijeka and he was answering. They were covering Dubravica and Krizancevo Selo, and they were coming from Rijeka and that's also where he was responding with fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you could also note on that day, on the 16th of April, that not only did the Vitezovi take part in the military operation, but there were also soldiers from the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Naturally. If there were about 100, 120 Vitezovi at the moment and over 300 troops, then it's evident who was there. Only the Vitez Brigade could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You noted that there was a concerted action on the part of the Vitezovi, the Jokers, and the Vitez Brigade against the area of Stari Vitez on that day, on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I can't tell you about the Jokers, but I can tell you about the Vitez Brigade and the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: They were responsible for the attack on Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: According to you, Mr. Breljas, members of the Vitezovi, did they take part in the attack on Ahmici on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, they did not, except perhaps some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You say "no, except ..." So there could have been some Vitezovi who went to fight in Ahmici on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I cannot claim that with certainty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein has an objection.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I cannot claim that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We're within the realm of speculation, and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, if you could establish a foundation with the witness what he knows and how he knows about where the various units were that day. Perhaps I could begin by asking this: Whereabouts was the command post of Mr. Plavcic, where you were that day?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: The command post was above the Kalen, the petrol pump, in a private house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In which area?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Krizancevo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, according to the information that you received or conversation that you heard between Vitezovi members, were there some soldiers, were there some units of the Vitezovi who took part in the attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, I could not really claim that with any certainty, I would not really affirm that, but there could have been two who used to live below there, that is, below Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And how did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: What information do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: According to which two soldiers from the Vitezovi might have participated in the attack on Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Because one is right beneath Ahmici, and on that date he was in Dubravica, and the other one, I didn't see him in Dubravica under the command of Mr. Marinko Plavcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Sorry, I do not really wish to mention the names of soldiers because they bore no responsibility for anything. Only their commanders, only their superiors may bear the responsibility under all the rules and all the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What you told us, I understand that it was the personal initiative of those soldiers, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the course of that particular day, the 16th of April, you received the instructions to abandon the command post at Krizancevo Selo and go to the school at Dubravica and to take care of captured individuals or prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As you went to the school in Dubravica, you could note there were quite a number of dead bodies and very many Muslim houses on fire in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, listen, I'm not from Vitez, I'm not from there. There were houses on fire. But were they Muslim houses? I mean, I know that only through the support of the artillery of the Vitez Brigade, Marinko Plavcic asked that his house be aimed at because there was a Muslim on his house, and he said, "That is my house. Fire at it because there's a Muslim up there."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There was a sniper, a Muslim sniper on his house that day?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is what he assumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As you went to the school and when you arrived at the school, you could see that there were several hundred persons, Muslim persons, who were being held prisoner in that school.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And a large number of them were women and children.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: There were men too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And there were between 300 and 400 prisoners there at that moment.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, no, not 400, I know that, but a little less. Around 350, slightly over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And those prisoners, were they detained in the gymnasium of the school, then in the basement, and in four classrooms?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Women and children were in classrooms, and men and some women who would not separate from their husbands and their children, they were in the gymnasium. Prisoners in the cellar, they were not those prisoners. Those were military prisoners, and they were separated from all the other prisoners who had also been brought there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Those military prisoners that you mentioned, could you give us a figure? Could you put a number to them? How many of them were there, more or less?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, they came there on various occasions, so I can give you a complete number of them, and that is 20, and at that particular moment there were four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The people you are telling us about, these 350 prisoners or somewhat more, were detained in the school until mid May 1993, were they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Even after that date. They were there until they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you say that they were detained until they were killed, what do you mean? Those prisoners were liberated; they were not all killed, were they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can clarify that. Which of the prisoners were killed? I don't want the names. Was it of a particular type, Mr. Breljas?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No. They were prisoners who were captured near Bobasi. First there were three civilians who apparently pretended to be military men, but in fact they were civilians who wanted to buy some food. One person was a craftsman in the Vitez Hotel where the headquarters of the Vitezovi was located, and he was a craftsman there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: We will come back to some of the detainees who were killed a little later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, it's now time for a break, if that's convenient. We'll adjourn now until half past.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, we are going to go back to the conditions of detention of the prisoners in the Dubravica school. You told us that these persons were held in the gym, in four classrooms, and in the basement. You tried to extend aid with the means that you had at your disposal. You gave them clothes, food, some bottles of water, and also some hay to sleep on. But nevertheless, you said that the conditions of detention were far from good.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: They were not good in the basement. The conditions there were appalling. However, in the gym there were very many people, not enough air. As for water, I didn't give them bottles, but across the corridor they had a toilet and they could use the tap water. The women and the children had somewhat better conditions because they were moved from the gym to rooms where, after all, the situation was more tolerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The detainees could not receive any medical aid, and the food was quite inadequate; was it not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You designated certain prisoners for trench-digging, and you did so at the request, according to your own hierarchy within the Vitezovi, or at the request of a representative of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, they came to collect people for digging, and so Marinko Plavcic and myself, sometimes he, sometimes I, would say, "We needed ten men for digging," and we'd tell them, "You get together ten people," and we'd send them off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As regards the instructions for the designation of prisoners that you received from the Vitez Brigade, they came from several people, and specifically you mentioned the person Mile Vinac, who was a member of the brigade command. And you also mentioned an officer in the brigade known as Zabac or Frog, I think in your language?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is true that Vinac would come. As for Zabac, he didn't come to pick the persons. He just came and took them off. But he didn't select them. There were no orders they could give us. He would just say, "I need ten workers," and he would take them off -- take them with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you receive any written orders from the Vitez Brigade regarding the selection of prisoners for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No. No. That was not possible. The Vitez Brigade could not give any such orders to Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The prisoners we are talking about who had to dig trenches, as far as you recollect, had to do so in the regions of Buhine Kuce, Bobasi, Kula, Krizancevo Selo, Zabrdze?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, you see, in those days I was still rather new. I know for certain that they went to Buhine Kuce and Krizancevo Selo. At that time I didn't know that they went to Bobasi, but I learnt later that they did go to Bobasi, Zabrdze and other places. But at the time I only knew of Buhine Kuce and Krizancevo Selo and Cucica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You said that these prisoners also received little food; they were sometimes mistreated and beaten by the guards.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, and I opposed this. And at our meetings I expressed my opposition. The food was limited for everyone, but they were totally without food. In fact, they would share one can among two prisoners. I don't know how the Vitez Brigade fed its prisoners. I know that I did give some cans occasionally. And there were instances of people being mistreated. And if I could have, I would have taken them to court. Some soldiers, but I don't wish to give their names, would tie the prisoners in chains, forcing the prisoner to bark and bite another prisoner, in response to which this other prisoner would kick him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were also informed that some of those prisoners were used as human shields, where they were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I couldn't describe this as a human shield, even though, according to all rules, it is a human shield. What they did, they put the workers in front of the soldiers. So there wasn't any real intention to use them as a human shield, but according to the rules of war this was contrary to those rules, where the soldier should come first and the workers behind the soldiers. But in this case it was the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You protested on a number of occasions, but apparently this produced no results?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, no one paid any attention to this. In fact, they declared me to be a fool. And, "What was I showing off about?", they would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Where did you protest against the bad treatment of prisoners in general and this kind of behaviour in particular?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: The only opportunity I had was to complain to the commander of the operative zone of Vitez, the IPD officer, information and propaganda officer, IPD.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: We have already referred to this issue prior to the break, that is the issue of the prisoners that were killed during detention by your unit. You said that, as far as you know, some 15 prisoners under the responsibility of the Vitezovi were killed?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You also knew that there was a practice applied by some soldiers in your unit to cut off ears of members of the BiH Army. You heard about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: This occurred in all units in the Vitez area. There were soldiers who resorted to this kind of practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You remember that a member of the Vitezovi brought you two ears one day and said that you should give this to Kraljevic for a snack?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Not two ears, one ear. He said, "Take it to Kraljevic for a snack."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There was another member of the Vitezovi whom you said would occasionally wear a garland of ears around his neck.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He didn't wear it. He made this garland. Let me remember whether he was there. I think that his combat group was not on the positions at the time. They were in the process of preparation for combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the period from the 17th to the 20th of April 1993, Darko Kraljevic, your commander, issued orders that should the army offensive continue, that the Dubravica school should be blown up together with the prisoners held there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He didn't just say that, but this had been prepared, the mining of the school at Dubravica normally, with all the people inside, whoever was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There were about 200 kilograms of explosives that were placed around the school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but there was quite a lot of explosive, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Sometime around the 20th of April the Armija launched an offensive against the school; the Vitezovi put up a defence line; the area was bombed; and you noted that at a certain point in time the Armija withdrew?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, the BiH Army -- yes, you could call it the BiH Army from Poculica and from other places, they attacked and they reached about 100 to 150 metres from the entrance to the school. Then the Vitezovi managed to push them back again and they retreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you have the feeling at the time that the BiH Army stopped its offensive because it was aware of the presence of these prisoners in the school and the risk that existed of the building being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't answer what the BiH Army did. What was in their minds is a matter for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, in your opinion, the resistance put up by the Vitezovi around the school, was that the only explanation for the suspension of the army offensive?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, I could not agree with that, because according to my military expertise the Vitezovi were weak to repulse such an attack. I think it was either the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina that gave instructions not to attack or the reason was that the explosives had been placed around the school and that a catastrophe might occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is precisely the point which I had in mind. The witness can't say what was in the mind of the army. It was -- it's for them to say. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Sometime in May 1993, Mr. Breljas, members of your unit, Nikola and Jako Krizanac, captured Kemal Poricanan, a judge from the region of Travnik, together with his driver called Jasenko; you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, if there's no dispute about this evidence, it can be taken fairly shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The judge Poricanan and his driver were killed during their detention, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And as far as you know, their bodies were thrown into the Lasva River.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you also remember that the judge was to have been filmed by a cameraman and that this film was to be shown later on, and in view of the condition of the judge who was beaten, you asked your superior for a postponement so that he would be presentable before the cameras; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. He was in the cellar, and to assist him -- he had been very badly beaten up, his ribs had been broken -- and to help him, I told Darko Kraljevic that he could only die in the cellar, that he had to be transferred to a room and to a bed and that he had to be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you remember the person who was going to film the judge with a camera?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I don't know him. I saw him when he was filming, when they came, but I really don't know his name, nor do I know who he is. He was just a man who came to make the film, and he actually did film him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did he belong to a team of cameramen from the Vitez zone placed at the disposal of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Not among those that I knew. He may have been someone I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On November the 1st, 1993, you organised a ceremony in memory of the members of the Vitezovi who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, this was the Day of the Dead, and I prepared the ceremony for the dead Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic and Cerkez attended the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: To be able to take a decision, I lit three large candles. On one I put the commander of the special purpose Vitezovi, commander of the Vitez Brigade, and commander of the Operative Zone Vitez, for each of them to come and light those candles. Mario Cerkez came to light his, but Mr. Blaskic sent his IPD officer instead of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez was unable to exercise the functions of brigade commander after the end of October 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Later, after that, he was commander for sometime after that. He stopped being commander when, at Grobcic, the BH army infiltrated themselves and destroyed 32 soldiers. That is when he was deprived of his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you indicate with greater precision the date when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I think it was the first week of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In December 1993 then.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As far as you know, Mario Cerkez and Darko Kraljevic went to the same school and knew one another very well, they got on very well.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Whether they went to the same school and the same class, I don't know, but I do know that they knew each other very well because they came from the same place, the same village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did they meet often, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Quite certainly they did, but in wartime, between Darko Kraljevic and Mario Cerkez, there was a dispute as to who was the more important commander. That was the only disagreement between them. Everything else functioned normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On several occasions, you were able to note that it was Mr. Cerkez who provided Darko Kraljevic with fuel when he was short of it.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Not only did I note it but I was present when Darko Kraljevic picked up the telephone and talked to Cerkez, and then he said at the end, "We're old friends. Will you give me some fuel because I haven't got any?" and then he said, "Of course I will." I was quite close and I could hear this conversation.
