utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You told us that as far as you know the Vitezovi unit was not formally subordinated to the Vitez Brigade, but there was an agreement, according to which, for logistic reasons, the Vitezovi unit was sometimes called the 4th Battalion of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: If I may, I would have to give you a more detailed answer to make myself quite clear. The Vitezovi and the Vitez Brigade were absolutely the same unit, the only thing being that the Vitezovi were the assault units, the special troops, elite troops, whereas the Vitezovi [as interpreted] were defensive forces. There was some disagreement over the command. The command was disunited, but the troops, the Vitezovi, were the storm units of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there's a small error in the transcript. The distinction between the Vitezovi as the assault unit and special unit, "whereas the Vitezovi," it says again, but it should be "members of the Vitez Brigade were defensive forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You saw repeatedly that the Vitezovi and the Vitez Brigade acted jointly in the Vitez sector and that on those occasions, during such operations, the Vitezovi received instructions from Mario Cerkez who, in his turn, received them from the operative centre of Central Bosnia, that is, Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. I think it is clearly too leading a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, would you tell us how you understood the command structure to be involving these people, particularly Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I did not say -- I never said that Colonel Blaskic took part in it, but they were separated in the sense that they did not fight together and they couldn't because the Vitezovi PPD was a storm unit and the others were defence units. But they could not command the Vitezovi because Kraljevic would not let them. It was said where the Vitezovi would fight, along which route, and that had to be more difficult and it was in the operative zone of the military district of Vitez at Zavisna [phoen], and that is the only place where I think they had contact with the military district or, rather, Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to round off the question that was asked by the President, Judge May, could you tell the Chamber what was the position of Mr. Cerkez in this command structure.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez, in the first half, he commanded Vitez as a whole. In his operative zone, his operatives decided what would be cleansed, what would not, and what would happen. But the Vitezovi at that time would be directed at a certain segment, a certain part of the area which ought to be attacked, but such orders could be issued by Darko Kraljevic and only by Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Cerkez then issue orders to the Vitezovi or was that reserved only for Mr. Darko Kraljevic? Did they receive their orders from anyone but Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: You're quite right, because the Vitezovi would not obey him, would not do what they were told by him, except that I do not know whether he and Kraljevic would previously agree on an attack. He could not issue any direct orders to the Vitezovi, but he could not do that even though I would have liked him too. But perhaps the two of them agreed about these things together. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Breljas. When military operation would be organised in the command area of Mr. Mario Cerkez, it meant distributing sectors among individual units. Who would tell Darko Kraljevic where should the Vitezovi be employed?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic had a deputy commander who was sent to Vitezovi to destroy it, and that Dragan Vinac, Dragan Vinac, he received orders because Darko had already given in in 1993. He already realised that the war was not a fair war. He was a good soldier, perhaps a bit crude, but he was a good soldier. And he was already giving in, therefore, so as to take the command, Dragan Vinac, so as to take over the command. And he planted all his friends, the majors, like Plavcic, to be killed. And after Vinac there was also this gentleman, what was his name, we call him grey haired, the major, Sidi. He was a big master of Darko Kraljevic, but he was trying very seriously to push Darko Kraljevic in doing these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I think we need a correction in the question asked. I said, "Who could be issuing orders to Darko Kraljevic?" Rather it was "Dario Kordic," as the transcript said.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, such orders could have come from Mario Cerkez in the former half of 1993. In the second half 1993 only Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You know from your field experience that during military operations that we are talking about the Vitezovi as a rule proceeded to the -- to the plunder of individual houses, and there looted usually small valuables, small sized valuables. Following that, when the brigade units would arrive, each would be larger objects of value which would be taken away by the troops?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Vitezovi, as I have said, they were the storm troops and they would be the first ones to enter a locality. They were always on the front line. So whatever they collected, they collected. Some small things that you could pocket or put in your packsack or whatever. But as the others came, they would take out refrigerators and whatnot, and those who arrived last would take off roof tiles from the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour, the transcript should reflect on page 60, line 15 and 13, that the name is "Darko Kraljevic," not "Dario Kordic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So you are saying that there would be several waves of attack, if I could call it that, of attack and pillage. You said that Vitezovi would take small objects and that others would help themselves to larger objects. You say others. Who are they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I mean the Vitez Brigade and those units, the units of the Vitez Brigade, that is the rear units who came at the second wave. Vitezovi were the ones who would launch the first onslaught and who would start the street fighting. And when that would be over -- because Vitez Brigade was a slightly more regular and larger unit. And then the Vitez Brigade would come to establish order -- order -- not order, disorder, but also an order of some kind. And then they would collect whatever they would happen to lay their hands on. And then the refugees would come and would pick out houses as they pleased and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And when the Vitez soldiers, when you said took away refrigerators, furniture and things, I suppose they used some vehicles to do that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Vitezovi did not take those things away. This was done by those from the Vitez Brigade. Vitezovi would take smaller watches, gold, money, or they would take passenger cars, for instance, tractors, that is, things which were mobile. Otherwise with trucks, that was done by the Vitez Brigade. These were the ones. When these ones left, the other ones arrived with a truck -- loaded trucks and left. And the war was -- I mean, the attack was still raging on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You said that on the 18th of December 1993, you had a list of Vitezovi members who were killed in the conflict, at least on that particular date. I should like to show this document which you signed, which is Z13371. You were the one who drew up the document, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: True. And that is not a complete document. Two sheets are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There is a page with 33 names, I believe.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: The list had to be longer, because I would write in my report the fatalities, the casualties, and those who could fight. But these are dead. But the list is much longer. The list of the killed is much longer. I mean, those killed in combat. They were about 200 of them and, from what I can see here, there is only -- 80. Excuse me. And here we have only 33 names. So it must have been lost somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But you are confirming your signature, the signature at the end of the page?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is true. This is the seal of our unit and this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I should like also to look at another document, which is on the 10th of May 1993. And it is Z871,1. Z871,1. It is a document dated 10th of May 1993, signed by Major Dragan Vinac. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. It's true that it was signed by Vinac and this is Vinac's signature. That I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I should like to show now a third document, which is Z808. It is a list compiled on the 24th of April 1993, by your counterpart in the Vitez Brigade, that is the officer responsible for information and propaganda, Zvonimir Cilic, whom we already mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I see the -- that some of the names come from the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And as regards these three documents, Mr. Breljas, you yourself said that there are several names which appear on the list of the Vitez Brigade members, that is on this list of Cilic, and that these same names appear also on the other to a list of the Vitezovi unit. I can give you these five names. They are Lovro Kolak, Anto Franjic, Ivan Zuljevic, Vlado Frankjovic, Zoran Ramljak.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: As for the first four, from what I know, they were in Vitez and in Vitezovi. As for the fifth, I'm not sure because I do not have them on my files. I do know about one who was killed in the attack on Mahala, that is Stari Vitez, Mr. Ninko, and I wrote for him a report on the casualties. But when I came to the person who was sorting it out in the military district, I found it again. And she also said, "How could he be in two units, Vitezovi and here?" I said, "I don't know. I have been given orders and he was there and he was working, he was operating -- handling the motor launcher, and that is why I wrote his name down." And all of a sudden he turned up on the Vitezovi brigade list. So he seems to have been in both places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And from the diaries of the documents it seems that there was a certain confusion as for the membership of these soldiers, in which units did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what it would look like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the document which was signed by Mr. Dragan Vinac, which is Z871,1. Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And can you see in place number 2 and 3, two soldiers mentioned here as men killed in combat, one of them is Blaz Plavcic and the other one Goran Blazevic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, true. True.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: These two soldiers appear also on your list?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you said that they were killed on the 23rd of October, 1992, both of them. Do you know about the circumstances under which these soldiers, members of this unit, were killed?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know that, because I was not there at the time, why I put them -- the names here. In Vitezovi, complete chaos reigned, so I tried to collect all the odds and ends, and when I would find somebody, that somebody had been killed, I would list him down as killed from amongst the members of the Vitezovi. But I don't really know anything about it because there was no order in all these papers until I started filing the casualties, fatalities and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But do you know in what sector were the two of them killed?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I do know about late Mr. Plavcic, because he was my commander as brother. He was killed somewhere above Novi Travnik in a village, but I really wouldn't be able to give the name of the village. I know it is above Novi Travnik. And he described it to me, but I did not go there. And so I can't really know what the name of the place is. I know it is above Novi Travnik. It is said that they were -- they had a clash above Novi Travnik and it was in one of those villages that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, I should like to show the last document to the witness. It is Z1279. Mr. Breljas, will you please look at page 5 of the document. There is a paragraph 6 there. It is called "measures taken by the administration." Can you see the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And in this paragraph 6 there is a sub item 5 which relates to the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Listen, this is in English, and I'd rather have the translation of it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, yes. Yes, there is the original version in Serbo-Croatian, page 5, paragraph 6 and subparagraph 5.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Except I can't find it here. Four, five.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Can you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I do. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you recall if your unit was ordered to take to the front line soldiers of the Vitez Brigade who were refusing to fight?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That I do recall. I can't find it here, but I recall that very well indeed. And I even demonstrated against that. I immediately went to the district -- to the military district and said to put a stop to that, because it is not up to Vitezovi to go and try to round up men, but that would be only to undermine the name of the Vitezovi, because before that they had very high prestige. And that was meant to undermine it, to smear their image so that people would start hating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you remember the order itself which was issued to you at the time, and who did it come from?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No. I got the order. I know it came from the Vitez Brigade, that those who'd fled from the front line, that the Vitezovi should immediately proceed to action, round them up in their homes and force them back to the front line, but those were oral, those were verbal orders only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, this document is of the 31st of October, 1993. I merely wanted to draw your attention to the fact that on that date, as you told us a moment ago, Mario Cerkez was still the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: The 31st, yes, true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We've finished with the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, for the last time, as for your intervention as an interpreter at Kraljevic's request when a humanitarian convoy was blocked at the crossroads, at the intersection in Dubravica, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what happened when you were asked to interpret on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: A soldier came to the barracks and said, "We need an interpreter up there on the bridge to Vitez," and I went there. I saw there Mario Cerkez, there were a number of people in trucks, and I also saw a tank and a British -- rather, a U.N. APC there. And Mario Cerkez then told me that I should tell them that they could not proceed, because Darko Kraljevic also came and I was ready to obey him, and he said, "Tell them that they cannot move on," and I did to the Major, so I did say that to the Major and told Mr. Major, "My commander says that you may not move on or else they will turn their RPGs on you and fire," and then my commander, Darko Kraljevic, said, "And tell them that I must search the tanks." So I told them, will they allow us. They allowed us, and when he searched them all, then he told the commander of the Vitez Brigade, Mario Cerkez, "Tell us, what are we to do now, to let them go or what?" And Mario Cerkez said, "Oh, no, we're not letting them go." And then he said, "Right. Then I will take a fresh leave," and he said, "You wait here. Until I give you an order to withdraw, don't withdraw," and I told this to the Major. The Major went to sleep, and I went to a vehicle because the night had fallen in the meantime. So I was there until 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning in that vehicle, drowsing, sleeping, and then a soldier came and told me to let the APC or the tank go, and I went to the Major and said, "Major, you are free. You may go now."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And this convoy, where was it headed?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: It was the convoy which had been formed in Split and was due for Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to a large number of vehicles in that convoy?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: There is no living man who could explain it. You would need at least 30 or 40 men who were in different places because all of a sudden, this convoy was taken and nobody knows what went where. Something about 100 to 120 lorries went down to the explosive factory and were there, and the others were driven away, taken also in different directions, and nobody knows where is what. In my barracks, I found seven trucks and the rest, well, they were all over Vitez and the surrounding villages. They had been driven away to all sorts of places. I don't know how to explain it to you really.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: After these events in September 1993, you were able to see that Mario Cerkez and Colonel Blaskic participated together in the capture of the village of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Mario Cerkez and Colonel Blaskic were in a church near Mosunj. The artillery for the attack was on a hill above the explosives factory, and the attack was to start on Grbavica. That is the first and only attack strategically carried out in accordance with all rules of warfare. Only one man was killed, one civilian, by chance, and the Jokers ran into a minefield and didn't move any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The units that participated in this attack were the Vitezovi, the Vitez Brigade, and the Jokers.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. There may have been some others but I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And at the end of December 1993, Colonel Blaskic demanded the disbanding of the Vitezovi unit.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. This was after Christmas, just before the new year, we received orders. First we received congratulations from Mr. Ante Roso, the commander of Herceg-Bosna, he was newly appointed, and he expressed best wishes for Christmas and the new year. And immediately after that, they said that every soldier who was looting would be sent to prison and some executed, and eventually there was an order that the Vitezovi should be disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was that the first time that you heard this type of threat made against soldiers for misbehaviour?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the first time since I had joined those ranks that there was such a strict order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: A certain number of former members of the Vitezovi unit were integrated in the new brigade set up in Vitez that became the 3rd Guards Brigade of which the commander was Dragan Vinac, your former deputy commander; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He wasn't the commander but he was the deputy commander. The commander was -- I know the name but for the moment I can't recollect. He was the deputy and he was the founder of the Vitez Brigade. But the commander, I don't know exactly who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Breljas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have finished with the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, my name is Bob Stein. I represent Dario Kordic. If there's any question that I ask you that you don't understand, will you let me know?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I understand from papers supplied to us by the Office of the Prosecutor that you speak English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Greek.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Some Greek, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Italian.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Again, a little bit. Not very well, but a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And, of course, your native tongue, Croatian or B/C/S; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, you spoke with officials from the Prosecutor's office, did you not? Specifically, you spoke with them in March of 1998 between April -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You spent eight days with them altogether; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And during that interview, you spoke Bosnian and English; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Listen, the Bosnian language is really the Serbo-Croatian language, but very well, let's make it Bosnian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. In any event, sir, during that eight-day interview with representatives from the Prosecutor's office, they told you that they were going to ask you a series of questions and that some of your answers may, in fact, make you a war criminal; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And, indeed, they warned you about your rights against incriminating yourself, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: They said -- but I told them, "I am not afraid of it. I have nothing to be afraid of. I am speaking the truth and I have nothing to fear."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Then let me ask you this, sir: At the end of your statement, and I would like to hand that to you now, there's room for your signature. Take a look at the back page, please. There's room for your signature, is there not, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. But now I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But you didn't sign it, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Listen, I don't know. Whatever I was given to sign, I signed, whatever was translated to me. I don't know what document this is. You have to explain to me what this is so that I would know. I did sign some documents, but I don't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, take a look at the front page, sir. This is the document that you participated in in March of 1998, an interview. Sir, if you look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I don't know how I did not sign this. I signed whatever I was supposed to sign, and about this, I am not clear how this was not also handed in to me to sign. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In any event, sir, you were given an opportunity to read that statement before testifying today; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And everything said in that statement is true and correct; isn't that so, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I don't know in this one, but in the one that was read back to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. During your meeting before your testimony with the Prosecutor, didn't they give you the opportunity to look at that statement and read it and make corrections to it if you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. This was during the investigation, not in the court. They asked me to correct anything I had to correct, and then after that everything was regular and whatever I was told, that was in there and that is what I signed. I don't know what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: If I understand your answer, sir, when these investigators from the ICTY were done with you in March of 1998, they went through this with you, gave you an opportunity to correct it, you made no corrections, and it stands as a true and correct document; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Similarly, in November of 1996, November 7 to be specific, you also gave a statement --

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: -- and that was to the Bosnian authorities. I'd like to give you a copy of that statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, if anything --

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- if anything turns on these documents, we shall need copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I have them for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Everything you told the Bosnian authorities is also correct and true; yes, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct and true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And last, you appeared before the Bosnia-Herzegovina Presidency State Commission for Gathering Facts on War Crimes and told them the truth too, did you not? And that would have been in February 1998.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is not correct. I did say some things but that was only two pages, the basic things that they were interested in. They were interested in the looting of the convoy and some minor things, and this is what I told them, and it amounted to only two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And here are those two pages, sir. My point being that everything in these two pages is true and correct; yes? That's your signature on the last page, is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, but this only states that I would give a statement. But when I got -- when I made contact with the War Crimes Tribunal, I stopped that, I never went there and never gave a statement after that. Q That two-page statement before you is true and correct; is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, those two pages. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you were picked up -- strike that. Do I understand that Colonel Stewart, Colonel Robert Stewart, passed you on the road to Vitez and then later picked you up there and took you to Vitez in April of 1993. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is when I had gone to Zenica on one occasion, and on the way back from Zenica he picked me up. At that time already, that was the time when Zivko Totic was arrested. That was actually that very day. That was the day when he picked me up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I understand that Colonel Stewart picked you up after he had actually passed by you once and told you to wait there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Because the shooting had already started and also the shelling, and I was up at Sljivcica, and that was in the Muslim territory, and I realised that I was in trouble because I was late. I was in civilian clothes. And I said "Mr. Stewart" -- actually, I didn't address him like that. I said, "I am a Croat. Can you drop me to the Croatian border?" He said, "Yes." I had to go to Zenica then. On the way back I helped him remove several anti-tank mines. I did not move from that spot because I would have been killed had I done so, had I moved from that spot. So that when he returned, I ran into his jeep and came back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And he took you back to Vitez; is that correct? Colonel Stewart himself?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You sat with him in the jeep, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And I want to ask you again, sir, that was on April 16th, wasn't it, sir, the day after the Totic kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is not correct. It was on the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I put it to you -- by the way, to make this examination easier, may we have Z2781,2, the map. Perhaps we can use ours. Would you put this on the ELMO, please. Now, would you point out for us, sir, Vitez on the map? It's in the lower left-hand side. You can look to your right. It might be easier for you. Did I say it right? I meant left.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, right. Here is Vitez. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You had been in Zenica; had you not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that was in the morning, in the morning around 10:00, 10.30. I was in the area where the new and the old Zenica have a boundary, and the units had already taken positions and did not let anyone cross. I managed to get across and arrive in Sljivcica where the fighting had already begun.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. So you had been to Zenica and you were travelling down the mountain road, were you not, to try to get back to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: To Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you were stopped in Poculica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That is when you first saw Colonel Stewart drive by; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He was coming from Vitez to Zenica, right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, from Vitez to Zenica. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And then, according to you, he picked you up on the way back and drove you to Vitez, right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You say that was on the 15th of April, the day that --

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Whether that was 15, 14 or 16, but it was on the very day when Zivko Totic was arrested, and I don't know when that was. I would like to request to ask me as little as possible about the dates and days, because those dates and those days I did not follow closely and I was not interested in that. But I know the facts. Zivko Totic had been arrested there, Colonel Stewart flew over to Zenica to intervene on that. A couple of hours later he drove back. He picked me up and three or four -- about three or four hours back in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fine, sir. Let me put it to you that Colonel Stewart in his statement to the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, this isn't going to assist, I suggest. Now we've spent quite a time on this. No doubt, the date can be established one way or another. What's the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My point is this, sir. According to Colonel Stewart, he stayed overnight in Zenica on 15 April, returned on 16 April, and so, according to the witness's testimony and dovetailing that to the Colonel's diary, Colonel Stewart picked this man up on 16 April at -- before 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Whichever day it was, the witness says that he can't remember the dates precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whichever date it was, what arises from it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What arises from it is allegedly he heard on the night of April 15, 16, in the early hours, conversations with Mr. Kordic and others relative to some plan. We dispute that, and indeed it is our position that he was not in Vitez or in the surrounds on 15 April. He did not get back to Vitez until 16 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "He" being?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: "He" being the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And again, for the record, and I think the record is plain on this, the Totic kidnapping occurred on 15 April in the early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: May I now answer this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you can answer if you want.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: First of all, it is not correct that Mr. Stewart went from Zenica to Vitez. Colonel Stewart went to Zenica in the morning. I was in a canal and I asked him. And he said, "I will pick you up on the way back." Three or four hours later he came back. And again I claim, and I can state under oath, that it was correct that not even three hours had passed between his going to Zenica and his return, because I helped him, when he was going from Vitez to Zenica, I helped him clear the mines which were in the middle in Sljivcica, and on the way back he picked me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, regardless of that, would you turn, please, to your statement given to the ICTY on March 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us have a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. Here you are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want this exhibited, Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No, it's just for Your Honour's edification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Turning to page 5 of the English, and that would be page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the interpreters get a copy or have the document placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We have extra copies for the interpreters. Page 4 of the Croatian, and maybe we could put it on the ELMO, although we will give the interpreters a copy at the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Follow along in your own statement, sir. It would be about the last -- next to last full paragraph. It says here: "About ten days after joining the Vitezovi, I, together with two Vitezovi scouts sent by Darko Kraljevic to Zenica, to gather intelligence about the Armija BiH. I spent about three days in Zenica to perform the job. I started back to Dubravica, Vitez, the same day when Zvonko Totic was taken prisoner and his bodyguards were killed. It was, I think, April 14, 1993. However, I could not make it beyond Cajdras, as I learned that shooting had broken out between the Vitezovi and those who were defending the Muslim village of Poculica from the assailant Vitezovi." I'll skip the next sentence. Then it says: "Getting to Cajdras at about 4.00 in the afternoon on April 15, I was stranded there until about 10.00 or 11.00 at night the same day. I spent the time at the church building in the Cajdras village. I had already sent two scouts across to Vitez through the woods and over the hills. In the evening of April 15, 1993, I set out from Cajdras towards Poculica on my way to Dubravica. As I neared the upper part of Poculica called Sljivcica, where a mosque is situated, I could see grenades being fired." I am going to skip a couple of lines because I want to get to the important thing: "I hid myself in a ditch near the road so that I would not be hit by a bullet. Fearing that I may be hit, I took out a paper and wrote, 'In case I am found dead, not killed by Bosnian Armija, but a stray bullet.' I spent a night in the ditch. The next day was, I think, April 15. At about 10.00 in the morning on April 15, 1993, I saw an UNPROFOR patrol approaching from the direction of Vitez to Zenica." And then the rest of the paragraph, sir, talks about Colonel Stewart clearing mines and then goes on to say: "By 2.00 in the afternoon the UNPROFOR patrol returned and I was taken to Vitez. I went to the barracks." Sir, again I put to you that Colonel Stewart, in his statement to the investigators of the ICTY, as well as in his contemporaneous journal, says that he spent the night in Zenica on 15 April and returned early in the morning hours of 16 April 1993. Therefore, sir, I say to you, you could not have been at the headquarters in Dubravica on the night of 15 April and the early morning hours of 16 April.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: It is absolutely impossible, but neither did I sleep in the ditch. I spent about three to four hours in the ditch. And it is absolutely impossible that he could have picked me up in the morning. He could only have picked me up, even if it was 1.00 p.m., but it would have been impossible to -- it to have been in the morning, because I started out in the morning after 10.00 a.m. from Zenica in the direction of Vitez. I arrived at Sljivcica where fierce shooting had already broken out. I had to hide in this ditch, and I spent there three to four hours. And even that is too long. But let's say it was four hours. And Mr. Stewart on that very same day went to Zenica and came back from Zenica. I can state that with -- and take full responsibility for it. Because the next day I realised that down there, when I went down to the bakery, which was across -- there was a ramp there with the soldiers, the HVO soldiers. That morning they had left the positions. I did not find them there. And that day was when the war took place, and that was on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to debate this issue. When Colonel Stewart testifies next week, we will point him out -- point the Colonel to his ICTY statement at page 5 for these issues. Now, sir, do I take it that you contend that as an IPD officer you had the rank of lieutenant; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: These were informal ranks, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time they were not official ranks. The people were given promotions on the basis of your rank. I was counted as a lieutenant and so I was a lieutenant. And later on the late Franjo Tudjman verified this rank in order for it to be officially recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, on this issue, without debating it, I again would point Your Honours to the record of Mr. Tuka's testimony on November 22nd, 1999, day 89, line 16 through 17, that there were no ranks. And Witness “Z.”'s testimony on December 6, 1999, day 99, at line 81, in a conversation with Blaskic she had again stated there were no official ranks. If this is a convenient time, it is for me, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll adjourn. Mr. Breljas, we are going to adjourn now for the lunch adjournment until half past 2.00. Could you remember in this adjournment, and any others there may be, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. And of course don't let anybody speak to you about it. And that does include the members of the Prosecution. Could you be back, please, at half past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood your direction. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1 p.m. 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, there's just one matter I want to ask the legal officer. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, there are a couple of things from this morning's testimony in the response to questions from the Prosecutor that I want to clear up. Would you please have in front of you the November 7, 1996 statement that you gave. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It looks like this. It looks like this.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, this morning you told us that at the end of March 1993 you met Dario Kordic in Tisovac outside of Busovaca and you asked him whether he could give you an assignment within the HVO forces, and that's at page 19 of the LiveNote. Yet, I want you to take a look at your November 7, 1996 statement at the first -- I'm sorry, the third full paragraph after the word "Statement," and you tell the public officials in 1996 that: "It was only on 17 February 1993, after a couple of attempts, that I managed to reach Kiseljak. Upon my arrival in Kiseljak, I spent seven days in a barracks, and since I made reference to my acquaintance with Dario Kordic, I think the people in charge of the barracks informed him, so that on 1 March 1993 I was assigned to RR wartime duties in the Vitezovi Special Task Force PPN in Vitez." In fact, sir, you didn't meet Mr. Kordic at all in terms of getting an assignment to join the HVO; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, it is not true. It is true that I had a very hard time getting out because I wanted to go to Sarajevo. I knew that the HOS was not fighting against the BH army. It is quite true that I came and that for awhile I was in the Vitezovi barracks, not some other barracks but the Vitezovi barracks. At that time, I was just a plain civilian, an ordinary civilian. I was lying in a room, and then after that, I went and saw Mr. Dario Kordic. I cannot claim with any certainty that Dario Kordic would remember me from before, but I did to begin with because I am a photographer in a photograph shop, his pictures were developed, and then the second time I saw him, it was in 1992 -- or 1989, rather, on St. Anthony's Day. He delivered a speech in Busovaca next to the St. Anthony's church.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me be more clear. You, of your own personal information or knowledge, do not know whether or not Dario Kordic in any way helped you get into the HVO; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, he did help me, sure he did, because he determined which direction I should take.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You don't know of your own personal knowledge whether he made any calls on your behalf, wrote any letters on your behalf. All you know is he said, "Go out --"

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. All you know is he basically went off and said, "Go see Darko Kraljevic"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, one other thing I was confused by, Mr. Lopez-Terres asked you whether your date of birth was 16 January, 1940. Is that your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No. The 18th of January. He said "19th" and I tried to rectify it but I had no time. The 18th of January, 1940.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I thought earlier this morning you told us you were born in April of 1940.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, but you couldn't hear it from me. Not 1944, 1940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, 1940 was the date which I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, the 1940 we don't quibble with, Your Honour. It's the April versus January issue that I'm looking at now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness probably can give the best evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: At page 18 of the LiveNote, we have "18 April." So my question again, sir: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: You could not find that, because what I know, and I know it from my early childhood, the 18th of January, 1940, one day after St. Ante Pavelic. I hope I've explained it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Take a look at the document that's in front of you, the 7 November 1996 record. That shows your personal identification number is "16-01-1940," and then there's some other numbers. Sir, you and I both can agree that "16-01-1940" is to be the 16th day of January, 1940; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: It is right. In 1996, when I came to Sarajevo, it is quite true, and that is why I requested that it be rectified. I went there and asked them to do that, and they said, "Oh, yes, of course, we shall change it." But that was an error, I had it in my identity card, and in a way I thought that perhaps it was a deliberate error so that I would have to come again to fetch my identity card -- well, be that as it may, but they couldn't find it anywhere because even my personal number said "18" rather than "16," at least that is how it was before the war. Now, I don't know, because as of 1991, everybody did as he pleased. So I just don't know now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, as of 1998, your personal identification number was also "16-01-1940" and then some other numbers identical to that which is in your November 7 statement; isn't that correct, sir? Take a look at the official note from February 16, 1998. You'll see it right in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That, I do not have to look at because I was regularly registered in two places. In Dubrovnik, that is one, and all the original documents are with me. My Dubrovnik identity card and my Dubrovnik driving license and my passport say the 18th of January, 1940, and my personal number is 18-01-1940. These are, yes, the first numbers of one's personal number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's move along, sir. The duties of the IPD officers were to take care of prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, not only that. I did that along with some other jobs. I had different duties at the PPN Vitezovi because Dragan Vinac did not want me to accept some soldiers who were his bosses before the war. So that I looked after the prisoners of war and after soldiers and I did all sorts of things, and I really think I had to play the jack of all trades there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. I didn't mean to say that was your only duty. My point is IPD officers, as I understand from your statement and testimony, were in charge of prisoners; they were liaisons with the various other military units; they were in charge of logistics; and they were also in charge of the general education of soldiers and morale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, it is not. IPD officer was responsible only for deciding on what kind of a soldier one was, whether the soldiers had carried out an order wrong, whether they behaved correctly or not, and things like that. An IPD officer had to have a board and say: This such and such soldier has committed this and that mistake; such and such officer has committed this kind of error. That was the official IPD's duty. And other IPD's has nothing to do with that, about prisoners. All they could say was whether the prisoners were treated properly or not. They did not have any other men. I was there. I was with Medecins Sans Frontieres because I could speak English, and I interpreted there and I did that. But that was not my duty. An IPD officer was there to say whether soldiers were properly behaving themselves and about the status of prisoners. That was all, normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, sir, with respect, the IPD officers also dealt with the morale of each of the units; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you sensitised the soldiers to the Geneva Conventions; did you not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Not soldiers, because soldiers could not understand it. But, yes, with some soldiers, yes, I told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to be picky about this, but if you take a look at your statements given to the officers and agents of the ICTY on page 15, the third paragraph from the top: "Within the units IPD officers were responsible for the general education and instruction of the soldiers in the units. An IPD officer would instruct a soldier in his responsibilities in the combat, his conduct towards others and sensitise them to the Geneva Conventions. IPD officers and units were also responsible for receiving orders from the IPD officer of the military district office and to impart the instructions contained in those orders to the soldiers of the units. I also dealt with issues concerning morale." That was your statement to the Tribunal investigators in 1998. Do you agree with that or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is what I just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, from that description, can we agree that the IPD officers were military officers?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, military officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They weren't political officers; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: They were a bridge between the military and the politicians. They were that bridge who from -- who were bridged over the distance, the gap between the political circles and military circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your IPD officers and yourself certainly had no say in political decisions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Quite correct. Only transmission of political messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Any orders that came to the IPD officers came from military superiors; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The IPD officers met weekly with the head of the IPD for the military district; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: On several occasions, in fact, you met with Colonel Blaskic as commander of the district; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I did. I was really pestering him. I was badgering him by telephone, because I wanted to keep him informed about certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a little while. My point is, sir, when the IPD officers met weekly, occasionally Colonel Blaskic himself would arrive? Yes?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He would send his IPD officer to these meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. It was always his IPD officer who was there. I mean, he would chair such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Dario Kordic never attended any of these IPD meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, as I understand again from your statement to the ICTY investigators, your unit was organised with three lieutenants, one captain, three majors and one colonel; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That was in the early days. When I was there, there were two colonels, three majors, two Captains, four lieutenants. And there were several sergeants, I don't know how many, five, six perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In any event, whether it was earlier or later, all of these officers or all of these ranks were military ranks; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And they all had military duties; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And Darko Kraljevic appointed you as the IPD officer because of your English literacy; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Among other things. And also because I was the eldest there, that is, I was 22, 24 years senior to the oldest one of the others. And I suppose he realised that. He trusted me, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. You had his confidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Because I drew his attention to certain things, to show him how some majors of his were laying traps for him so as to ruin his military career.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: On the other hand, he would bypass you whenever there were any dirty dealings afoot, because of your principled attitudes; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: It is, and he did it several times. And then -- and then I told him, "Darko, you don't have to bypass me. I'll tell you whether you should do something or shouldn't do something, whether something is ethical or not, but do not listen to everybody," because I notice there are spies in units. They wanted to ruin him. He was a great name in the Vitez area and he was a good and honest man. Except that he was an unrefined man and he did not have enough imagination, enough education to think of things. But he always performed what he set out to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to turn our attention, if I can, to the names of the combat units. You mentioned earlier this morning Puma and Wolf and others. Am I correct that you also said at times the names of the combat units would change?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly now, in the year 2000, you wouldn't be able to give us the dates or the name changes as they occurred while you were with the HVO, would you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No way. It was temporary. I think the names were changed about two times. I believe Puma's changed. Wolf stayed Wolves 'til the end. And the Puma, I think, and the Foxes changed their names, or perhaps Foxes only. At any rate, I believe units changed about twice and then they would revert to their original name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. And you can't help us with what the names of the units were before you joined the Vitezovi, can you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I could tell you about three months back, but not before that, because that name they had throughout, I believe ever since the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, additionally, besides the names of the units, the soldiers themselves had call signs; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I don't understand that question. What kind of calling signs do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic at one point, for instance, his call sign was 21, and his artillery commander was 18. Does that remind you of the call signs we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I see now. Now I understand. Vitezovi were not all that trained to think in that way. They had a somewhat lower rank of communication in their operational work. Say, if one of those squads or something that would get away, they would call Puma 1, Puma 2, or if they split into three groups, it would be Puma 1, 2 and 3. I mean, it was -- after all, Mr. Blaskic was the only strategist who was in Vitez, and he had these things organised in a more sophisticated manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I don't want to make a big deal out of this. My point being that there were individual soldiers who had individual numbers as their call sign, such as Blaskic, number 21; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, those figures, as I told you, during an attack or something like that, of course they would have it. They would have a code name or the figure that was on their Motorolas, for instance, which they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And those code names and figures changed over time as well; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Once I requested and proposed to Colonel Darko Kraljevic: If they did it, they had not done it and had realised it was necessary. That is, if a soldier from that combat group were captured, then this would immediately have to be changed because, naturally, this one, the captured one, would start singing sooner or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That brings me to my next point. During your tenure with the HVO in Vitez, 1200 members of the HVO Vitez Brigade were killed in 1993; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I don't know how many. The latest information I received was when we were issuing some money to the families of the fatalities, and I had 84 families to see and they had 800. So once there, IPD officer Cilic had said, "No problem for you. You have 80 of them," and I said, "Well, it was easy for you because you had 10 younger women who did it for you." And I had to do it all by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me help you sir. Turning to page 19 of your statement to the ICTY in March of 1998, at the fourth full paragraph. And in the Croatian version it would be on page 16, and it would be the last paragraph. About midway through the paragraph: "1200 members of the Vitez HVO brigade had been killed in the course of 1993. I know that at some time, when I received assistance for the bereaved families of 180 dead soldiers of Vitezovi, while Zvonko Cilic, brigade IPD officer, received similar assistance for the 1200 soldiers of the brigade who had fallen in fight."

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is not true. I never said that anywhere. All I said was that we had been given the same amount that we were then to give, and it was 50 marks. I never said it -- he was issued the same amount of money. It was per soldier, the same amount per soldier, the same kind of money that I would pay to my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, it's a very simple point. 1200 soldiers had fallen; are you denying that? Are you denying you said that? Take a look at your Croatian version on page 16, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you, because I do not know how many fell. According to him, he had 800 fatalities. And I wasn't there, I wasn't a political officer with them to have the list of their killed. I had the list of mine killed, so I can say how many men were killed with us; that it wasn't 880 but, rather, 984, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right, sir. In any event, let's take another point you made during your direct examination. And that was relative to the relationship between Dario Kordic and Darko Kraljevic. You never heard Darko Kraljevic get an order from Dario Kordic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You never read an order from Darko Kraljevic -- I'm sorry, from Dario Kordic to Mr. Kraljevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I only heard a telephone conversation once about something. I can't tell what it was about, but he did speak to Mr. Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So Kraljevic spoke to Kordic once, a conversation you couldn't hear, and from that you concluded that Kordic gave orders to Kraljevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He couldn't give orders to Kraljevic, he could just inform him about something that needed to be done, and Kraljevic was the one who gave orders. Kraljevic could not be given orders, that is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So regardless of what the relationship was between Kraljevic and Kordic, Kraljevic did not take orders from Kordic, military orders from Kordic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I cannot say that he did or he did not. In my judgement and according to my knowledge, he carried out operations which only Kordic could have conceived. Now, whether he gave him orders or not, whether they met -- I know he went to Busovaca. Whether he went to see Kordic or someone else, I don't know. I didn't see them meet, but the operations that were carried out could only have been planned by Dario Kordic and no one else at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you conclude that without ever seeing a piece of paper or hearing a direct order or plan; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: A piece of paper in the area of Vitez until sometime around the 15th of July, 1993, no one issued to anyone nor paid any attention to. There were just oral orders, instructions. There was a total split, a disunity within the military. Everyone did whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, let me try it a different way. You said, in your judgement and according to your knowledge, Kraljevic carried out operations which only Kordic could have conceived. Do you have any facts on which you can base this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I do. The first fact is that Darko Kraljevic was the protector of 30 Muslim families and he protected them against everyone. No one could touch them. Secondly, whenever I spoke to Darko Kraljevic, he never conceived of any operation that would be done in such a way, that we would attack from this side or that, but he always had the final act. He was just the perpetrator, the person who executed a certain operation, but not the person who conceived it or strategically organised it. He never did that, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn your attention to something else. In December of 1993, specifically 22 December through 24 December, there was a major offensive in Krizancevo Selo; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the Muslims cut through the Croat lines; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Seventy Croats were killed at least; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Not more than 30 soldiers were killed on the outside. But five of them -- three were killed in a traffic accident when a commander of the Vitez Brigade, a lower level commander, was driving two members of the Vitezovi in a Mercedes, they turned over and they were killed in a traffic accident, and then again Krizanac and maybe some ten or so soldiers. So all in all, there were not more than 30 people killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In any event, whether there were 30 or 70, Colonel Blaskic immediately arrived in the area and stayed in the Lasva Valley until January 1st, 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic was not in the Vitez district. He was in Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You're saying he did not arrive in the Lasva Valley at the end of December 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No. I have evidence to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, you claim that Mr. Kordic was seen by you poring over some military orders right around this time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I didn't see him issuing orders. I saw him debating with the commander of the Vitez Brigade over a map. I never said that he issued orders because Colonel Kordic did not have the military expertise to be able to issue orders. He just collected information from zonal commanders and he drew on their expertise and on their knowledge to say okay. He had no military knowledge personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You indicated to the folks at the ICTY that Mr. Kordic fashioned himself a colonel; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is how we called him. He was a colonel. He was a colonel because there was no higher rank than colonel in that military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, you told specifically the officers of the ICTY, at page 22 of your statement to them, page 19 at the Croatian, at the top of the page, first paragraph: "Despite his camouflage military-fashioned attire and despite the fact that Kordic fancied styling himself as a colonel, he was an ignoramus in military matters"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, during this particular period of time, you point to the episode that you talked about on direct examination and you give an example of Kordic going over a map with the group commanders, and you say: "I saw Kordic conferring with some combat group commander over a map. The commander was trying to explain how he was going to counterattack. One could see that Kordic was completely out of his depth and did not have many intelligent questions to ask. 'Okay. Okay. Go ahead' was his perfunctory response." You told that to the members of the ICTY; did you not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, and that is correct. That is what I have been saying just now. I repeat the same, that he was conferring with him, and when this one explained to him -- I knew this person too up to a point, and though I thought it was all wrong, and this attack on Krizancevo Selo was not an attack in the proper sense, it was in response to a challenge, because before that when Colonel Blaskic went to Mostar --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: None of that is my point. My point is simply this: Mr. Kordic, although he was given the title of colonel, in your opinion was not a military man; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He was a military person because there was no one else. He was the most respected person in the military district of Vitez, and he performed those duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, sir, he didn't give you any military commands, did he?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Of course not. I was so small, I was so far below him that I couldn't receive orders from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you, of your own personal knowledge, have no evidence that he gave a military command to anyone; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He headed the operation against Krizancevo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's it? That's the only evidence that you have of him issuing a military command, that he was in the command post poring over maps?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you wanted salaries for your men, you didn't go to Dario Kordic to get salaries, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I did want to go to see him when I got to Posusje, but he was the person who could do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, sir, with respect, turning to your ICTY statement, at page 17, at the bottom, third paragraph from the top -- I'm sorry, third paragraph from the bottom, and that would be on the Croatian at page 14, you say: "In my request for Vitezovi soldiers' salaries, I next approached Lieutenant-General Milivoj Petkovic. He was kind enough to respond immediately to the situation and ordered that sums amounting to two unspecified months' salaries be given to me according to the list that I had prepared." Do you remember going to Lieutenant-General Petkovic? That's at page 15 of your statement in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: First of all, this was not when I was in Vitez. This was after I had left Vitez. I went to Posusje because Colonel Darko Kraljevic had received some salaries, and our salaries were suspended for a whole year because we were surrounded, so each one went individually to pick them up. I didn't go directly to see Mr. Petkovic. I first looked for the defence minister, who was Mr. Soljic at the time, I wanted a meeting with him. It took me 15 days to reach him. I had a list of 420 men, and I never saw more than I don't know how many --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The issue is, to get salaries for your men, you went to Soljic and you went to Colonel Rupcic and then finally to Lieutenant-General Petkovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, as I understand it, again from your statement to the ICTY, Kraljevic specifically had you go to Kordic's press conferences and heckle him, ask strange questions, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that in reference to Kordic but rather to Blaskic, that I should try to provoke Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, take a look at your statement to the ICTY at page 35 in the English, third paragraph from the bottom, the Croatian version would be page 31: "I would regularly attend the weekly press conferences that were held on every Friday. I attended the press conferences through 1993 after I joined Vitezovi. Darko Kraljevic had told me to attend the conferences and to heckle Blaskic, Kordic, and the others as much as I could. Darko Kraljevic was elated when I would irk Blaskic and Kordic or others in the press conferences. Every time I would score a good point with them, and subsequently the conferences would be broadcast on the television, I would receive a bottle of whiskey and cigarettes from Darko. 'My IPD is shagging them well' he once remarked." That's what you told the ICTY when you chatted with them for eight days; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but this applied mostly to Mr. Blaskic. Though sometimes even when Valenta was there and if I managed to heckle him, he was glad, but he never said anything about Kostroman. And he liked to address questions to Mr. Kordic, but it was Mr. Blaskic that he aimed at most with these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You talked with the Prosecutor about military discipline and military courts, and I want to turn your attention to that. There was, in fact, a military prosecutor established in June of 1993; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, a court and a prosecutor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And there were four judges appointed as well.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell. I know that there were three. I don't know about the fourth. I know there was a public prosecutor, his assistant, and three judges. Whether there were three or four, I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I won't quibble with that. They were located at the civil police station building in Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, you see, I really don't know. It's a long building. At one end was the civilian police, but what was at the other end, I don't know. But in any event, it was in the same building as the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. The officers in your brigade had powers to punish. For instance, you could give two days' detention for violations, could you not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That was done only by the late Mr. Plavcic, and it wasn't for disorderly behaviour but because they brought guns from Rostovo. I wanted nicely, in a humane way, to transfer the Vitezovi under the command of Blaskic, but they appointed their own men to do this forcefully, by force, to force them there, and these people from Rostovo brought over quite a number of rifles, more than 30 of them, several thousand bullets, and of course I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, with respect, that's really not my point. My point is: You, as a commander, could give two days' detention for violations; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: In theory, yes, but nobody would do as I would tell them if I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And Darko Kraljevic could give 30 days' detention or forward a military violation to Colonel Blaskic if it was a serious one; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic, in the case of a serious infringement, would simply take a gun and kill the person, which he in fact did on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My question, sir, is under the military courts and under the military rules Kraljevic was entitled to detain somebody for 30 days or forward that individual to Blaskic for further punishment; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And Blaskic, indeed, could dismiss or give three months detention for those serious violations; isn't that right? Dismiss the soldier I should say.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, sir, because I cannot answer this. You are talking about peacetime rules. Wartime rules are a completely different case. If what I am commanded decides to execute a soldier, he has the right to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, again, turning to your ICTY statement at page 28, the second paragraph from the bottom, page 25 of the Croatian version, the first full paragraph at the top: "As far as powers to discipline and to punish are concerned, my powers to punish the Vitezovi soldiers extended to awarding a maximum of two days detention in the barracks. Darko Kraljevic could award a maximum of one month's detention. If the commander deemed the gravity of the breach or offence in question to be deserving of a greater sentence than one month's detention, then the case file had to be forwarded to the commander of the military district, Tihomir Blaskic, whose powers to punish extended to awarding a maximum of three months' detention beyond which he could forward the case to the military Prosecutor. The commanders also had powers to dismiss delinquent soldiers from their position." That's what you told the ICTY investigating team; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I am saying again that this was based on the rules applicable when there was no state of war. However, when there is a state of war, the method of punishment changes completely. Because in a state of war you cannot wait for 10 days, 15 days or 20 days. There are situations when you have to punish immediately, and there are other situations when you can wait, so that wartime circumstances differ completely from peacetime circumstances. And I was saying this on the basis of peacetime military rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Furthermore, sir, we can agree, can we not, that under the military rules a commander was bound under law to initiate criminal proceedings against soldiers who had been guilty of commission of crimes and to forward the case to the military Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
