utterances.text: Yes, he was obliged to do that. Yes, he was under obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The military prosecutor was a man named Marinko; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Marinko, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And he was subordinate to Blaskic in rank; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm afraid my question probably wasn't clear. Blaskic had a higher rank than Marinko; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Marinko didn't have a rank. He was the public prosecutor, and every morning he had a meeting with Blaskic to agree on what they would do that day. They had a meeting every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My point is, in 1993 military discipline was meted out by military personnel either, as you say, in the field or through the system we just talked about; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: You are talking about the second half of 1993 and not the first half. In the first half there was no law, there were no rules. People did what they wanted, people killed each other, plundered, looted. But you are talking about the second half, when Colonel Blaskic already had achieved a certain degree of immunity and was proclaimed the commander of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Then during the second half of 1993, the process of military discipline was as we just discussed, and it was military discipline handed out by military men on military matters; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, indeed, because of that situation --

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: -- you complained on countless times to the military district IPD officer and to Blaskic, informing them that the soldiers of the Vitezovi would leave the barracks without permission and other kinds of disciplinary actions you wanted to have taken; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Only when I spoke to Blaskic about this. This was just in conversation. But officially I address his IPD officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right. And, in fact, every week you made at least 10 complaints about the misconduct of the Vitezovi soldiers to the IPD officer at the weekly meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I may have said 10. Sometimes there was three or four, sometimes five, sometimes 10. It wasn't always 10 complaints. There would have been five or six. Sometimes there were none. Once I didn't submit a report and I was told off because of it. I didn't -- I just hadn't had enough time to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, you went to Blaskic dozens of times and explained to him that the Vitezovi soldiers were looting and murdering without any authorisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Not members of the Vitezovi, but individual members of the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I am not sure I understand the difference, sir. Let me turn to your ICTY statement at page 29, next to the last paragraph: "I went to Blaskic dozens of times and explained to him that Vitezovi soldiers were looting and murdering without any authorisation, but to no avail. By the end of the war he would not even consent to see me. Blaskic did not even once punish any of my soldiers, even though I informed him of their bad conduct many times." That was your statement; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, but only once did he punish Darko Kraljevic. This was sometime in August or September. He asked him as a punishment to bring seven rifles. Darko Kraljevic called me up and asked me to find several rifles and take them to the military district, and I did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. We will get on more quickly, Mr. Breljas, if you just listen to the questions and just answer them as quickly as you can. And in that way we'll get through your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, sir, on December 23rd, 1993, you received an order from General Ante Roso from Mostar in which the General said something to the effect that, "Any soldier found guilty of looting, robbery, raping, burning or causing other damage to the property, would be sentenced to a minimum of five years imprisonment and a maximum of capital punishment." And that would be on page 30 of your Croatian statement, the second full paragraph. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Just following up on one other thing about the way the military units of yours worked. All orders addressed by Blaskic to the Vitezovi were received by the IPD -- by you as the IPD officer; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, most of them. The majority were received by me. Perhaps one or two went somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I want to switch gears a small bit. You were asked by the members of the ICTY investigating group to define a civilian or what is a civilian. You found a difficulty, based on your experiences in 1993 with the HVO, to define a civilian; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, to a degree. But excuse me, Your Honours, I cannot but not take into account that you may be blaming me, so I have to take a longer lead in order to explain how I got there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we get onto that, is there any relevance in this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes. I'll follow it up very quickly, sir, and I'll be much more precise. The defenders of Stari Vitez were both women and children; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: In a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And, indeed, there were snipers who were women; in fact one was a very good shot, as you described in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That was not in Stari Vitez. It was a woman from Zenica who operated in the area of Poculica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Poculica is a Muslim village; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: There were snipers from the Mahala section of Vitez; were there not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to make sure here, and we are coming towards the end. You were asked specific -- specifically asked to send prisoners to dig trenches; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you simply followed those orders; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, but not literally. I could explain what I mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, according to your statement, you, quote: "Sent 23 prisoners for trench-digging. I was simply following Marinko, Plavcic's order." My question to you, sir, is: In addition to the civilians who were digging trenches, military people were also digging trenches; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Not the Vitezovi. Not the Vitezovi, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fine. But other units of the military were involved in trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, those military units which were the reserve ones, but not the storm troops. No soldier would use them for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, relative to the judge, who you told us about in your direct examination, you never complained to Kordic about this judge or his confinement; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But you did complain to Blaskic about it, correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lopez-Terres brought up that you were in Canada and had some problems with the law. Let me ask you this: Your first problem with the law was when you had problems with your stepfather who called you an Ustashas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, now, Mr. Stein, I wonder how this is going to help the Trial Chamber. It's all a very long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, it's pure credibility, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These events are 20 plus years ago, so I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We'll bring them up to current times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to stop you, but you need to bear in mind that this is -- please don't interrupt. This is not a jury trial and I don't think we were assisted by what we heard already. Unless there is something specific about this witness which you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, regardless of the tiff you had with your stepfather -- let me direct your attention. You had a tiff with a police officer and left Croatia in 1972; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, that was during the hot summer that there was a revolution going on in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Then you went to Canada, where you had the scuffle with the Croat priest and were jailed for three months. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I first went to Greece, and then from Greece I went to Canada. And I was in Winnipeg, that took me about six to eight months to get to Winnipeg, and then there in Winnipeg I had an altercation with a priest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Then you were in the United States between 1976 and 1981; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you use your own name?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, my own name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Were you given a social security number?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, and a green card. I believe that it's still somewhere around.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me ask you as a final question, because I've been curious by this: You, as I understand your testimony, because of your principled attitudes, were disgusted by what you had seen in your tour with the Vitezovi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, because I saw things that are not becoming of the worst rabble, let alone Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yet, in 1998 and 1999, you went to the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina to prove your status as a member of the PPN Vitezovi and to get a supplement to your salary; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is not correct. That was not the purpose of my going there, but, rather, to meet with Palavra and to discuss my status. But, as I was contemplating of approaching the ICTY, I wanted to see what they knew about me, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Money was not a topic of discussion at all?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you are as positive of that as the rest of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: What do you mean? I obviously went and asked to be compensated for what I was owed. Of course I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So money was part of the conversation, and you were there to be compensated for what --

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: It was my money.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: -- for your work with the Vitezovi; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Mr. Breljas, good afternoon, my name is Bozidar Kovacic, along with my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, who is seated left of me, represent the Defence of Mr. Cerkez. And I also have several questions for you. If you could please limit yourself to answering them as briefly as possible. And since we are both speaking the same language, would you please pause before you start answering a question after you have heard it, so that we can proceed in an orderly fashion.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Breljas, on several occasions during your evidence you made allusions to your experience, to your knowledge. You said that you had knowledge of the strategic sciences, of the law, and some other areas of expertise. So I will just ask you very briefly about your education and experience. Firstly, you said that you completed your elementary school in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then you completed your secondary schooling in Ruma; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what you specialised in?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I started off with mining, but then I interrupted that because of all this Ustashas business, and then I went and did it through the evening school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So are you saying that this was in Serbia, but that there was a mixed Serbian and Croatian student body, and because of your ethnic belonging you were persecuted?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. And that also followed me in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So those were the two technical secondary schools. You did not go to the high school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I paid for those exams and I did them privately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then you said that you went to the school for political science in Zagreb. You failed there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We checked your background and you never went to go to the -- to pass the entrance exams?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I checked, but they told me that I shouldn't even try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you didn't even try?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No. No. I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So then you went and did your national service?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The former JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What branch of the armed forces were you in?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I was in the airforce as a driver and I was a personal driver to General Viktor Bubanj and another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever get any education of the customs and laws of war?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No. I did something on my own. I did my own -- those studies of strategy and history. I got a fairly wide knowledge of history, and also I did some military law. That I did on my own because I did not have any financial assistance or my own means to do it formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After you left the JNA, did you make an arrangement with the Secret Service of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You had no contacts with the military Secret Service?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And during your stay abroad?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You told us about the period of the breakup of Yugoslavia, how you came back to Sarajevo, and you never specified where you were for a whole year after the death of Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: This was not in Kiseljak. Blaz Kraljevic was killed after the holiday in August, and I was there in 1992, in March, at my mother's birthplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, you were outside of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I was outside of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Regarding Blaz Kraljevic, could you just tell us who he was so that everybody knows?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: He was someone who had a large military unit. He fought against the Serbs, he would use the Croatian territory for that, and he was more or less one of the chief commanders of the HOS and he was one of the first who started the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we agree that he was with the HOS and that he fought in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, and he was killed at Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Darko Kraljevic, your subsequent commander, was any relation to Blaz Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, there was no relation. But his units, Darko Kraljevic's units, were HOS units at first before they became the HVO, and Blaz Kraljevic at that time financed him, supported his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In your statements to the ICTY investigators of 1998, which has been referred to a number of times here, you also mentioned the story about Blaz Kraljevic, but there is something which is not quite clear. Were you able to join the HOS units during the period when Blaz Kraljevic was still alive?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Of course. How else could I have been at Dalj or Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How about in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, except I came to Dubrovnik and then I stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When did you come to Dubrovnik and with what military?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I was a civilian, in fact, in Kupari, and Blaz Kraljevic was active in that area. Then from there, I went to Trebinje and I believe that was in April or May 1992. I could not tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I still am not clear. What was your function there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Listen, you know very well that the HOS were broken up until mid 1992, and I was looking for a unit which I would join. I was at Vukovar's, I was in Zagreb with Mr. Karakas whom I told that there was a radio transmitter in Dalj --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's leave that alone.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: How shall I leave it alone if you want me to explain something? If you don't want me to, then please don't ask me such a question. I was just an independent soldier, a friend of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Karakas. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Mr. Karakas was one of the deputies of Mr. Spegelj who was the defence minister, one of his assistants. Now, what specifically he was, I don't know, but I reached him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. To clear up any confusion here, are you sure this was Mr. Karakas or Mr. Kikas?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I'm sure this was Mr. Karakas because people were looking for him and they specifically said "Mr. Karakas".

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you parted ways with him too, you were not happy with him.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I said he wanted me -- I was looking for a type of telephone which I never got.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I went to Osijek to go to Glavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this was 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned this type of phone. You said that this was -- does that have anything to do with intelligence?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Listen, I have covered a lot of ground and I have come to know things that I should not have known. My father was killed, and I studied all kinds of sciences so that I would come to -- and I studied a lot to find who I was, where I belonged, criminal sciences, history, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You spoke about ranks, what ranks were used. You said that your commander, Mr. Darko Kraljevic, was a colonel, and we saw a document evidencing that. Do you know whether any ranks existed in the HVO, or more specifically in the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but they were not official ranks. Certain commanders of combat groups or some other commanders had patches with ranks, and it would be "123," or "Colonel," "Major," "Lieutenant," "Captain," whereas we did not. We were just told, "You are a Captain. You are a Lieutenant. You are a Major," but officially, according to the law, only Mr. Tudjman could verify, that is, confirm any ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, based on what you told us yourself, you must have handled a number of written orders which arrived in your unit, the Vitezovi, from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command issued by Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: In the latter part of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In any of those orders, did you see that any person there, any addressee, was marked by rank?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I wrote a number of orders myself, and I always signed it as Lieutenant Breljas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas, could you just focus on the question, please. You were referring to the Vitezovi, but I was referring to the documents coming from the Operative Zone and you referred to it as headquarters or the military district. Have you ever seen Mr. Blaskic signing any of his orders and including his rank?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I never paid any attention. I was not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's an answer too. Could you tell me, did you ever see a written order signed by Mr. Cerkez, who is present here?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You never did? You never had an opportunity?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have any opportunity to hear that anyone addressed Mr. Cerkez by using his rank?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. I did, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That was colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That was around the 1st of November, 1993. When he came to light the candle, I addressed him, I said, "Colonel, this is your candle."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that we've never heard this before.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I don't know whether you've heard this before, and you couldn't have heard it because you were in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that this was in November 1993. Let me ask you, before November 1993, did you ever have an opportunity to personally meet with Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When was this, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: This was when the convoy was stopped; that was the Convoy of Salvation for Tuzla. He was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And how did you address him then?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is an answer too.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I don't know whether I had addressed him at all -- oh, yes, he asked me something and I told him that Darko had arrived. At that time, I was only taking orders from Darko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. We're not going to go into that. But you don't know whether any ranks existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, from your evidence, it would appear that you were given a rank of lieutenant but more importantly a position of the IPD officer about ten days after you joined up.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, 10, maybe 15, maybe even 20. But I arrived there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time, you were a brand new person there in the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely new.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Nobody knew you from before?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, no one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. A little later on, you assumed the duties of the logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes. When I saw what Jozo Buha was doing, then I threw him out and took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So did you now carry out two different duties?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you did other things, like this candle lighting and then doing payrolls, and all this reminds me of something else. So let me ask you: Did the Vitezovi as a unit have an official for the social affairs?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No. That was only established in the headquarters, this is how I called them, in Vitez later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the Vitezovi had it in mid 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, no, no. This was in the military district of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How about the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That was the duty of the IPD officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to another area. In the beginning, when asked by the Prosecutor, you said that you were convicted in Canada, and I was not clear. You were sentenced by a Canadian court, not by -- it wasn't some administrative punishment.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a Canadian court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Based on the investigation we conducted, we received information that you first came into contact with the Vitezovi unit at the time of the attack on the gas station in Kalem. Firstly, do you recall this incident when the gas station in Vitez was attacked? It was called Kalem.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Of course I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this was on 16 April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No. It was attacked before the 16th of April, but on the 16th of April it was completely taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that during the fighting around this gas station a member of the Vitezovi, whose name was Kozina, shot at you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is not correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I was just passing by on the road where the fiercest shooting was going on, and later on he said, "I saw you with a bag on your head. I had you clearly in my sight. I almost killed you. I had a clear shot but I didn't shoot."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that the attack started before the 16th. When you said so, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Illegally; that is, they were getting ready to take over the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But what you said, you seemed to have been in Travnik, where you went --

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Not Travnik, Zenica. But I knew that they were getting ready for the attack on the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean before your departure?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, before my departure, because that was the first feature that was to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So Kozina almost killed you by mistake, and this is what he told you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That's what he told me. He said he had me clearly in his sights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that the Vitezovi then held you or detained you, and it was the first time, they did not know you before then.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That is not possible because I was an interpreter, I interpreted on that very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this is not true. Okay. We're moving on. During your stay in Vitez, did you establish any closer contacts with a woman?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was lodging with a woman called Kata who lived across from Dragan Vinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is that Kata Rajic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you lodged with her?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you had good relations with her?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You could say that you had an intimate relationship with her.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I don't have to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you left there in early 1994, when you left Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, in April 1994, the 15th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you meet her when you were back in Vitez on two occasions in 1996 and 1997, when you wanted to sort out your rights and in order to receive further compensation?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you manage to put your name down on those lists which were being compiled in order to get veteran's compensation?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, and I received two salaries. Because I was not in Vitez, I received from the social affairs office an envelope with those two additional salaries, and these were for 1993. But I did receive those two salary amounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And besides that, you also tried to get your name enrolled in the rosters drawn up by the BH Federation in order to gain the right to some transformation rights; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you succeed in that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that you spent the night at Mrs. Kata Rajic's, that you were put up there, but then you also said that at first, when you arrived in Vitez, you would stay and spend the nights in the school.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, during the first two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you mean during all that confusion in the early days of the war?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is then that you are in the school.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, I'd always lived in the school, except that I would go to her and she would do my laundry, and I came and went as I wanted. But most of the time I spent in the school, in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But before that you also stayed with the next-door neighbour of Kata, with a lady called Mrs. Mira Pocrnja.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes, I spent about a fortnight with her and then I moved on to Kata's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that she threw you out of your house because you inflicted injuries on here?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Sir, I do not think I'm going to discuss these matters with you because this is none of your concern. It is my personal matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. But you lived there with her?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I may have and I may have not. None of your business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you took photographs of all the members of the Vitezovi, or at least most of them?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Not true. Not true. Only dead. I only tried to photograph the dead ones, and I took photographs of almost all of the dead so that their parents could have pictures. Two of those who had lost their military cards, I took photographs of two living soldiers just so that they could get their documents right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You became an IPD officer about ten days after you arrived. It was Darko who appointed you.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: It could have been 15 days. Now, deputy IPD, because at that time Mr. Marinko Plavcic, Major Marinko Plavcic, was the chief IPD officer, and I was appointed as his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. And it was Darko Kraljevic who told you that, who told you so.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You did not receive any letter of assignment.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I mean, something in writing.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Well, naturally, I was issued a document as a lieutenant of PPN Vitezovi, an IPD officer, so it was all in writing, and I was issued the same thing from Kostroman in writing from when to when I was there, because Kostroman was the superior commander for the IPD, Mr. Ignac Kostroman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I'm afraid my question was not clear enough. This morning, in the document Z1075, it is the 18th of June, and that was still a wild time, that is, when there were no documents. All of a sudden we see a perfectly formatted document which appoints, designates Colonel Darko Kraljevic as the deputy head of the SIS centre in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, or rather you said 10 or 15 days, so it could have been late April or early May that same year, you were appointed as IPD by Darko. At the time of your appointment, or within a few days of that moment, were you issued with a document appointing you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Naturally, I automatically got into the staff where Dragan Vinac, Kraljevic, Miso Mijic, majors, and a logistician, Buha, and Shanta [phoen], IPD officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe you explained it all to us. What I'm asking you is not whether you became a member of the command. You told us that. But were you issued that document appointing you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. What kind of a document; if I was appointed -- if I am on the list of the command, if I was issued a military document as such. What else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, will you please look here. Will you please look in this direction. This is a document which was signed by Miso Mijic, who appoints Darko Kraljevic to such and such post, that is deputy head. Were you issued with a similar document whereby Darko Kraljevic appoints you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: Sir, you are referring to the top most officer, and the most prominent post of Croats in Bosnia, and you want them to issue something to me holding the lowest rank in the army. And of course I wasn't issued it by them. I was issued that by Kostroman. And of course I have this document amongst my documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What kind of document?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That Anto Breljas, officer with Vitezovi IPD.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: He wrote "PD"?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: That's true. So that is his. That is where it comes from, Mr. Kostroman, for Colonel Kostroman, the I am on the files as such and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But that was later?

utterances.speaker: ANTO BRELJAS
utterances.text: No, that was the confirmation of my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you don't have anything from the term of appointment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am now going to interrupt. We have been going around this point, Mr. Kovacic. I understand why. We've now got an answer. It's seven minutes past 4.00 and we would wish, if at all possible, to finish this evidence today. Are you going to be very much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not able to reorganise my notes, my original notes, which I planned for this witness, and with the situation after my colleague's time. So it's difficult to tell, but I guess perhaps an hour and a half, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, nobody so far has been an hour and a half, or if so, it hasn't been much longer. We'll adjourn now, but could you please try and shorten things for the morning. The witness has only given evidence for about an hour and a half on both the previous examinations, and he only, I think, mentioned your client once. I may be wrong, but my recollection is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I have a couple of minutes of your time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may just -- certainly, Your Honour, I will do my best and I will restrict myself only to the parts where the witness was referring to my witness. Probably some contra point as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Tomorrow morning. Mr. Breljas, could you please be back tomorrow morning at half past 9.00 in order to conclude your evidence. I am sorry, it's not been possible to conclude it today, but we will conclude it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to go now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I just wonder if I could seek some guidance from the Chamber in relation to witnesses either this week or next week. I didn't list next week's witnesses when I first dealt with administrative manners this morning, but for the four days we've got next week, we've got Colonel Stewart, who is not likely to be a particularly short witness. It's been noted that both defendants wanted to be here. We've got the witness who seeks protective measures, who was referred to by an earlier witness -- yes, by Payam Akhavan, you will remember, was coming because of matters raised with him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He should be fairly short.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He should be fairly short. You've got a substantial witness who, I think, is seeking protective measures, but comes, as it were, from the other side of the conflict, was listed from the beginning. And one other fairly short witness. So we've got for next week, for four days, probably enough witnesses for at least three, or three plus of those days, and it may be for all four days. And if the Chamber isn't going to be sitting next week, because of the representations made this morning, I will start the process of cancelling them now, rather than later. If the Chamber is going to be sitting, I want to see if I want to have another witness on standby, given that I forecast the subpoenaed witness won't be turning up and will be dealt with shortly. As to this week, I haven't been able to contact the witness (redacted) -- well, another witness who could give evidence on Wednesday without any controversy, because the defendants are willing for him to give evidence. We haven't been able to raise him by telephone. The Chamber has only -- recently had Beese to look at. The other two witnesses, neither of them are particularly long, but I don't think we will get through both of them tomorrow. They are likely to take us into Wednesday at the very least. And it may be that it would be a prudent course not to try and squeeze another witness in on Wednesday afternoon, when he could, perhaps, not be concluded. And it might be possible to use, say, Wednesday afternoon for arguments about some of the dossiers that have been served, if those arguments can be dealt with by a Chamber of two Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I rather doubt that it would seem sensible not to get another witness, I should have thought, unless we could be certain of finishing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Beese, I think it unlikely, and I speak purely for myself, it's unlikely that we would be prepared to hear him this week or next, given the Defence's argument about time. As for the witnesses for next week, we have not yet resolved that matter, but we will give you an answer as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So with all the shifting around, what is the batting order for this week and next week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt you can be told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll tell him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, half past 9.00 tomorrow, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.15 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of January, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
